summary: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax under the provisions of the Wealth Tax Act. The assessee had filed an assessment for the assessment year 1962-63 on the total income of Rs. 1,10,000/-. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer and dismissed the appeal. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended that the net wealth of the assessee was not taxable in the hands of the Hindu undivided families but was assessed as a result of the partition of the family. The High Court held that the income from the property was assessable under the Wealth tax Act for the relevant assessment year and accordingly, the question was answered in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The net wealth is not taxable as a right but only as a liability. [675 H] 1.2 The net assets of an assessee are to be taken into account in determining his net wealth. The value of all the assets belonging to the assessee on the valuation date is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the assessing officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date. [650 H] 2.1 There is no provision in the Wealth Act for determining the net assets. The net value of the assets is determined according to sub sections (I), (II) and (III) of section 7 as the valuation dates are not relevant for the purpose of determining the assets of the person on the date of the assessment. [663 H] 3.2 In the instant case, the assessee had claimed that the value of net wealth should be taken in the sum of Rs 1, 10,000/- and not in the amount of net assets as a whole. The Wealth Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant on the ground that the total assets were not taxable. [664 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 2.2.1987 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in S.T.C. Nos. 1 of 1988. V.R. Reddy, B.D. Sharma and P.K. Balasubrahmanyam for the Appellant. M. Veerappa, A.S. Nambiar, R.N. Poddar, Mrs. K. Rajitha, Ms. Jaya Kumari, Ms Urbhana Rao, Ms Anuparna Rao, S.V.Rangarajan, P.P. Rao and B.Kondalar for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. These appeals are directed against the judgment dated 2nd February 1987 of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh in Income Tax Reference No. 1/1988. The appellant is a Hindu Undivided Family. He filed an application under Section 7 of the Act for assessment of his total income as a Hindu family. In the said application, he claimed that he was assessed by the Wealth-tax Officer as a loss and that the sum payable to the Hindu Undivided family was not liable to be included in the net value. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal referred the following question of law arising out of its order dated 2th February 1987: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, it is open to the assessing authority to determine the net income of the individual assessee as a partner of the firm at the time of his assessment." The High court answered the said question in favour o the Revenue. Hence these appeals by special Leave. 2. Shri V.K Reddy, learned counsel for the appellant, submitted that the wealth tax officer was not competent to determine his net income under Section 8(1)(i) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act").

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the Central Reserve Police Force (in short 'C.I.F.) on 25.5.1971 and he was dismissed from service on 2.6.1972. The respondent filed an application before the Tribunal for reinstatement in service with full back wages. The Tribunal held that the respondent had been convicted by the criminal court on a charge of misconduct, and accordingly, imposed a penalty of dismissal from service upon him. On appeal, the High Court set aside t he order of the Tribunal and directed the appellant to reinstate the respondent in service. In this appeal, it is contended by Mr. S.K. Bagaria, learned counsel for the appe llant that the order of dismissal passed by the Tribunal was not based on any evidence or on a consideration of the facts of the case. The High Court has held that there was no material to show that the departmental enquiry officer had been fair and proper in imposing the penalty. It is further contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the disciplinary authority could not have imposed a lesser penalty than the one imposed on the respondent. In support of this contention, the learned counsel placed reliance on the decision of this Court in Union of India vs Tulsiram Patel , ; ; (AIR 1962 SC 814). The question whether the order passed by an Industrial Tribunal imposing a lesser punishment was based on evidence or not, was considered by this Court and it was held that if the respondent was found to have been guilty, it could not be said t hat he was not in fact the person convicted. In the present case, the respondent did not make any attempt to prove that he was guilty of misconduct. The order of penalty imposed on him was based upon evidence which had l eaving the way for the Tribunal to exercise its powers under s ection 25(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. It was held by this court in Union o f India vs Union of Indi a, ; , that if there is no material or evidence to show t he misconduct of the respondent, it can be said that the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authorit y was based only on the evidence and not on a finding which would be just and proper. In view of the aforesaid decisions, the order imposing the punishment passed by t he Tribunal cannot be sustained. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. He filed an application under section 8(2) of the Act for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The trial court held that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1)(e) of that Act. On appeal by the respondent, the Additional District Judge confirmed the order of the trial court. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the question whether defendant No. 1 was a " tenant" within the definition of section 4(2)(e), was not an issue which could be decided by the Mamlatdar under the Act and, therefore, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to decide the said question was barred by virtue of Section 58 (2) read with Section 58(2). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding, that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to pass any decree for possession against the appellant. [532E] 2.1 The question whether a person is a tenant or deemed tenant within section 4 (2)(a) of Act has to be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties and not on the other hand, the nature of the questions required to be determined for grant or refusal of relief claimed in the suit. [506F] 2:2 The question as to whether defendant no. 1 is a "tenant" within section 2 (1)(f) of Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939 was not decided by this Court and, accordingly, the High court was right. [504B] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant had been a deemed licensee under section 5 of the said Act. The question that arose for consideration in the present case was whether defendant Nos. 1 to 4 were tenants within the purview of section 5(2), and if so, whether they were entitled to claim protection under section 58 (1) readwith Section 58 of the act. [436F] 3:3 The High court erred in not considering that the issue as to who was a ' tenant' within the ambit of section 58(1) of Chapter VI of the Tenancy Act was not considered by it and, consequently, the question of deemed licensee did not arise. [498A] 4. Section 58 is an enabling provision and it provides that where a person has been dispossessed from the land on or after 1st July, 1962, he shall be entitled to recover possession thereof in accordance with the provisions of the law as if the Act had not been passed. [500F] 5.1 There was no question of the High Courts taking into consideration the fact that the questions as to title were not decided on merits by this court and, hence, the decision of the case was not open to be considered by the authorities under the provisions. [482C] 5:2 Section 58 does not apply in the instant cases because the question as regards deemed licensee was not raised before the High courts. The only question that was referred to the Mamlatdar was whether the question regarding deemed licensee could be determined by the Civil Courts and if it was not so, the Civil court had no power to decide that question.

The petitioners were appointed as casual workmen in the respondent-Corporation. They were engaged on daily wages and were paid minimum wages. The respondent- Corporation issued a notification under Section 4 of the Act, which was published in the Gazette on January 11, 1981. On the basis of the said notification, the petitioners were absorbed in the regular establishment of the respondent. The petitioners filed an application before the Central Government for regularisation of their services. The Central Government rejected the claim made by the petitioners. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to be regularised in service as they were working on daily wage and were not entitled to any minimum wages for equal work. [691B] 1.2 The petitioners were engaged as casual workers in the year 1981 and their services were terminated by the respondent on January 10, 1981 after a lapse of about two years. They cannot be denied the right to regularisation merely because they are working on the basis that they were employed by a company incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act]. [692C] 1:3 2.1 There is no material placed before us to show that the petitioners are being paid minimum wage for equal employment. The question whether the petitioners can be regularised or not does not arise in this case because the petitioners have been working on a daily wage. They are entitled for regularisation only as per the terms of their appointment. [650D] 2.2 There is nothing on record to show how the petitioners' services were comparable with the counterparts in the government service. The fact that they are being employed by an employer incorporated under Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does not mean that every workman in a department of the Government should be treated as a workman. [663F] 2:3 In the instant case, the respondent was working on January 9, 1981 and he was absorbed in regular establishment. The petitioner cannot be said to have been employed by the company incorporated within the meaning of Section 3(1) of the Minimum Wages Act. [664G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 16.3.1987 of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Calcutta in O.A. No. 8 of 1981. S.K. Kanojia, Ms. A. Subhashini and M.S. K. Nair for the Appellants. V.M. Tarkunde, Mrs. Arundhati Roy, Ms Anuparna Ghosh, Ms P. Dutta for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by B.P. JEEVAN REDDY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 16th March, 1987 passed by the Central Administrativ e Tribunal, Kolkata Bench in OJC No.8 of 1981 whereby the petition filed by the appellants under Article 32 of the Constitution was dismissed. The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of handicraft and were working as casual labourers in the office of the Assistant Engineer, Building Department, Government of West Bengal. They have been absorbed in their regular establishment in regular establishments. The respondents filed an appeal before the Tribunal against the order dated October 16, 1981 passed by it. The Tribunal dismissed the said appeal on the ground that the appellants were not being paid any minimum wage and they cannot be allowed to raise the same contentions as were raised in the said petition. The appellant is aggrieved by the judgment of the High court dismissing the writ petition filed against the Tribunal. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the respondent had been working as a casual labourer with the appellants since 1981 and, therefore, he was entitled to regularisation. It was further submitted that there was no material on record before the Industrial Tribunal to show why the petitioners should be regularised. The High Court has rightly dismissed the writ application filed by them. We are unable to accept the submission of the learned counsel.

The appellant, a minor, executed a will in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act for dissolution of his marriage on the ground that he had not executed the will and that the will was not genuine. The trial court held that the execution of the will by the testator was proved and accordingly decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and directed the appellant's suit to be dismissed. In this Court it was contended that the High court was in error in holding that the signature of the testatrix on the will could not be established as she had understood the nature and effect of the recitals in the preamble and the effect of its contents. It was further submitted that the evidence of the appellant was not sufficient to prove the execution and that it was not necessary for him to prove that the testatrix had understood her nature and purpose of the document. Held, that the trial court was right in holding the will to be genuine. In the instant case the High Curt has rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had understood and understood the terms of the deed. The High Court was also wrong in coming to the conclusion that the respondent had not proved that the document was executed by her. The learned trial judge was right. The will was duly proved before the court and it was rightly held by the High. Appeal allowed. 3) The appellant has now come up in appeal against the judgment of the High' Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court had correctly interpreted the document Ex. A to hold that the signatures of the deceased on the document were genuine. [775 H] (2) The execution of a will by itself is not conclusive proof of its execution and it can be proved only if the execution thereof was established. [750 B] (3) The evidence of this witness was not enough to prove execution of Ex.A to the satisfaction of the court. The appellant had not explained as to how she understood the contents of the Will. The evidence given by the appellant in this connection is not sufficient. [751 D] (4) The will executed by the deceased was not proved before her and it could be proved by examining any other person who could prove that it contained the true nature and object of the transaction. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1165 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 8, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in C. A. No. 966 of 1965. S. T. Desai, for the appellant. B. Sen, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The question involved in this appeal is whether the execution by the will executed on the basis that the testator had understood it and signed the will in question as a true copy of the same will was proved before it. The facts leading to the execution are not in dispute. The only point for consideration in this case is whether there was any evidence to prove Ex. B to the effect that the Will was executed on behalf of the testator or he had understood his nature and intention. [761 H; 771 A] (5) The question whether the will has been proved before a court does not arise in this matter. The execution by itself cannot be established unless the execution is proved.

The appellant, a dealer in motor vehicles, was carrying on business as a dealer under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The respondent, a registered dealer in respect of motor vehicles manufactured by it, purchased motor vehicles from its dealers and sold them to the purchasers for agricultural purposes. The sales tax authorities assessed the appellant to sales tax under the [Andhra Pradesh General sales Tax Act] on the ground that the goods were not "used" within the meaning of entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Andhra State Sales Tax, Act, 1956. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy and assessment contending that the tax was not payable by it under entry No..4 of Schedule I of the said Act. The High Court held that the sales were "used", within the scope of entry 4 of schedule 1 of that Act, and that the appellant was entitled to claim exemption from payment of sales tax on the goods manufactured by him. The State of Andhra Pradesh filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The expression "use" in entry No.,4 of schedule I of that act is used in the sense of "used". [675 H] (2) The word "use", as defined in entry 4, must be understood in a broad and wide sense so as to include not only the use of the motor vehicle but also the use thereof. [676 G] (3) The words "used for purposes" used in entry 5 of Schedule II of the Act are not intended to cover the goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. [775 H; 776 A] (4) The use of motor vehicle by a dealer for carrying goods for agricultural purpose is not a "use". It is only when a purchaser makes some other use of it, that he can claim exemption under entry 4. [750 B] (5) The question whether the goods are "used in connection with projectors" or "parts thereof" does not arise in this case because the appellant purchased motor vehicle from its dealer and sold it to the purchaser for agricultural use. [751 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1965. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1964 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petition No. 823 of 1963. S.T. Desai, R. Ganapathy Iyer and B. H. Dhebar, for the appellant. M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K.K. Venugopal, S. Balakrishnan, V.R. Krishna Iyer, S., P. Nayar, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Sikri, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 24, 1964 passed by the Andhra High Court answering the question referred to it in favour of the appellant and against the State of Madras. The facts leading up to this appeal are these: The appellant is a dealer registered under the Act. He purchased motor cars from its purchasers for use in connection therewith. The goods were manufactured by the appellant in his factory. The said goods were sold to the buyers for agricultural uses. The question that arose for consideration was whether the sales of motor cars were "useful" within entry No, 4 of the Schedule II and were therefore taxable under entry 5. [875 H-776 A]. The High court answered the question in favour o the appellant by holding that the sale of motor carbons was not a 'use' within entry 4 and that it was not used for any purpose other than agriculture. It is against this judgment that the present appeal has been filed. 2. The only point urged before us is whether the appellant is entitled to exemption under Entry 5 of the schedule II of that enactment. 3.

The petitioners are the owners of minor minerals. They were granted a Parwana for quarrying stone and stone in the State of Gujarat. The lease was executed by the State Government under the Rules. The petitioners applied for grant of quarry leases in respect of minor mineral. The State Government issued a notification on 26th March, 1976 under Rule 21 of the Rules for grant or renewal of mining leases in favour of the petitioners. On 30th April, 1977 the State government issued a Notification under Section 15 of the Act prohibiting quarrying of stone and minerals from any place in the area covered by the lease. The said Notification was published in the Government Gazette on 26-3-1977. The petitioner applied for renewal of the mining leases which were granted to him under the rules. On 3rd April, 1978 the State Govt. issued a fresh notification under Rule 20 of the rules declaring that the minor minerals specified in the Schedule to the Rules shall be liable to be removed from the leased area by the lessee or any other person who is not a Government lessee. The respondents filed an application for grant and renewal of quarry lease before the High Court. The High Court held that the petitioners were entitled to quarry stone and mineral from the land covered by mining leases and they were entitled for payment of royalty in accordance with the provisions of Rule 21. The appellants filed an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal holding that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. In this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the Act is a law for the purpose of implementing the policy of the State and the Act does not authorise the State to make a classification for purposes of implementing its policy under which the Rules are made. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964 were in force at the time when the Act was passed. [557F] 2. The object of the Rule is to ensure that the minerals specified therein are not removed from a place for quarrying and no royalty is payable by any person who has taken quarry Parwana or quarry lease in respect thereof. [506D] 3. The right conferred on the Government under Rule 15 is an absolute right and it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification of the minerals for purposes other than those specified in Rule 21 and the proviso to rule 21. [504F] 4. The Act does no doubt provide for a classification of minerals for the purposes of the proviso, but it does not authorize the State or the Government to make any classification for the said purpose. [500G] 5. The power to make rules is conferred on an authority competent to make such rules. The rule making authority has to exercise that power in accordance therewith. [525F] 6. The Rules do not authorise a subordinate authority to make the rules which are in the nature of subordinate legislation. [511D] 7. The proviso to Rule 21 does not empower the State, Government to frame rules for the matters specified therein. [54E] 8. The expression 'minerals' used in Rule 20 is wide enough to include minerals and minerals. [55G] 9. The word 'mining' used by the legislature in Rule 15 means 'to remove', 'or any other purpose'. [56F] 10. The words 'to carry out' in Rule 25 are wide enough not to confer a right on the State. [57H] 11. The rules do not authorize a subordinate or subordinate authority in making rules for carrying out the purposes mentioned therein. The legislature has no power to frame any such rules and the rule does not create any such power. [58F] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1979. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1977 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 1125 of 1976. S. T.

The appellant was a hereditary trustee of a temple. He died in the year 1948 and his widow, who was a minor, executed a will on April 1, 1949 bequeathing her properties to the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for partition claiming that he was a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not a hereditary trustees and that the succession opened in favour of the appellant by virtue of the will dated April 1. 1949. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the plaintiff was a person who had become a hereditary Trustee within the definition of section 2(9). The High Court further held that as the appellant had not become a member of the family under the Hindu law, he was not entitled to succeed to the office of trustee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that there was a vacancy and that it was a mere vacancy. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding otherwise. [557 D] 2. Section 6(8) of Act 19 of 1951 is not applicable to the facts of this case. It is true that the appointment of the trustee was made by the holder in office and he had no power to appoint any person as a trustee. But the fact that the trustee appointed was a member does not mean that the office must be held to be hereditary. The appointment of a person as trustee is an act of management and not a mere post. [657 D F] 3. Section 2(8)(a) of Hindu Law, which defines hereditary trustee in section 6 (9), provides that "the office shall be deemed to be a hereditary succession." It does not say that the vacancy must be filled by the appointment. The fact that there is a vacancy does not necessarily mean that it is a mere appointment. [650 D] 4. Section 3(8), which defines the term ' hereditary trustee' in section 2 (9) does not refer to an appointment of any person or a vacancy of a deceased person to another. It only refers to an act done by the person appointed as a Trustee. The word 'man' is defined in section 3(10). [650 F] 5. Section 4(8A) of this Act provides that the hereditary trustee shall be a member and the office shall vest in the successor. The words "or any other person" are not relevant to the question whether the appointment was made on the basis of an act or an appointment. It does, therefore, not mean merely that the act or appointment is a hereditary one. [643 D] 6. Section 5(8-A) provides that if the vacancy is filled by a person appointed in office as trustee, he shall be appointed to the vacancy and the vacancy shall be filled up by the successor in office. The expression 'or any person' occurring in section 4(9), therefore, means an appointment made on a vacancy. [641 D] 7. Section 8A of the Indian Trusts Act provides for the appointment by succession or nomination. It provides that where there is no hereditary trustee, the appointment shall be made to the successor and the appointment is made to any other office. [651 G] 8. The question whether a vacancy has been created in favour or not is a matter which falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court. [678 H; 69A] 9. Section 7(9)(a), as it stood prior to its amendment by Act 19/1951, provides that any appointment made under section 3 shall be subject to the provisions of Chapter III of the said Act. [69B] 10. The position in law is well settled that a vacancy can be filled only by the succession or appointment and not by appointment. In the present case, there was no vacancy.

The appellant was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi for an offence punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted him on the charge that he had committed murder of one Karunakaran and sentenced him to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. The State filed an appeal against the said judgment before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The evidence of PW 4 is not reliable. He was a witness who was present at the place of occurrence when he was in police custody. [775 H] 2.1 There is no material to show that the deceased was being chased by PWs 1, 2 and 3. It is also not established that the accused had any enmity with PWs 1 and 2. The evidence on record shows that PW 4 was present near his house when he went to the place where he was sleeping after the assault. The prosecution case is that PW4 was standing at a distance of about 100 persons from the place which was in the possession of the appellant. He had seen the accused running away from the spot after the attack. The other witnesses who were present at that time when he came to know about the murder of Karunakaran, were not examined by the prosecution. [750 H] 3.2 It is well settled that if a person is found in possession of some incriminating material, which is not only his personal property but also the evidence of any other person, it is open to the court to consider whether such person is guilty of an offence under Section 304 Part II or not.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer found that the assessee had received the amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- as salary from his employer and that the said amount was not liable to be taxed in the hands of his heirs and legal representatives. He held that the amount received by the assessee was not taxable in the assessment year under section 24B but was income received by him before his death and therefore he assessed the total income of the deceased. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that since the assessee did not have any income at all from the estate of the said deceased, the amount was liable to tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Act and accordingly the High Court set aside the order passed by the Tribunal. The Revenue filed an appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression "income" in sub section (1) of section 24A means income received or receivable by a person during his lifetime and it includes any amount which is received or deemed to be received by such person before his life time. [675 H] 2. The word "income " in the context of sub section(1) means income which may be deemed by fiction to have been received or accruing as a result of the death of the assessee and therefore they are not liable for tax under sub section 1 of section 4. [775 B] 3. Section 24B provides that the legal representatives of a deceased assessee shall, on his death, be entitled to receive in the prescribed manner any amount payable by him after his death. The liability for payment of income tax is thus limited only to the cases provided in sub sections 1 and 2 of section24B. [750 D] 4. Section 4(2) provides that where the assessee has received any salary or any legal representative, he shall be liable to pay income-tax on the total amount of his income as computed under sub sections (1), (2) and (3). [776 H] 5. The words "income tax" in section 24 B are wide enough to include any amount paid by a deceased person before the assessment or reassessment proceedings are initiated. [751 G] 6. Section 25B provides for payment by a Hindu Undivided Family of the value of his estate and not by the legal representative of the dead person. [75 H; 75 A] 7. The provisions of sub sections 2 and 3 of section 25B do not apply to the case in hand. [76 H; 76 B] 8. Section 26(1), as amended, provides that if any person dies before his lifetime, he is entitled to get his legal representatives who have been assessed to tax in the individual capacity. The legal representative has a right to receive the amount payable under section 25A and it cannot be said that he is not liable under sub-section 1 of Section 24 B. [77 H; 78 A] 9. Section 27(1A) provides for the payment by the deceased person of any amount due from him after the death or in the case of a Hindu joint family, to his legal representative and the legal heirs of the husband who is liable to make such payments are also liable to satisfy the tax liability under section 26B. The provision does not apply if the assessee dies before the death and he has no income at any time during the life time of the person. The amount payable to the deceased was not assessed in the personal capacity of the legal heir of the father but was assessed as income from his estate. [79 H; 80 A] 10. The appellant was appointed as a District Judge in the State of Andhra Pradesh. He was appointed to the post of District Judge on January 1, 1962. On March 31, 1963 he was promoted as District Judge and posted at Hyderabad. On April 30, 1963, he was transferred to Hyderabad. The Government of India issued an order dated May 3, 1963 under section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, appointing him as a district judge in the Union territory of Andhra. On June 1, 1964, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Government of Andhra on May 3. 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appointment of the appellant was not in accordance with law and he was not entitled to be appointed as District Judges. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred under section 4 of the Act is a legislative power and it cannot be exercised by Parliament or State Governments. [975 H] (2) The appointment of a district Judge in a State is made by the President in consultation with the High Courts. The power of the Central Government to make any law for the time being in force is not subject to the provisions of the Constitution. [ 976 B] (3) The expression 'any requirement' as used in section 3(1)(a) of the public Employment ( Requirements as to residence within that State or Union territory) and Rule 3 of Rules under it are ultra vires the Constitution and, therefore, Parliament has power to make such law. [1008 G] (6) The term 'any provision' as employed in section 5 of the Indian Employment (Organisation Act, 1956, is a well settled rule of interpretation that where the words used in a statute are capable of two constructions, one which would avoid the hardship to the other and the Court should not adopt an interpretation which will defeat the object of the legislation. The respondent, a minor, was appointed as a Constable in the Police Department of the State of Madhya Pradesh on December 31, 1978. He was served with a charge-sheet dated October 20, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Rules and he was asked to submit his explanation within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice. The respondent submitted his explanation on November 25, 1978 and also filed an application for inclusion in the electoral roll of the year 1978. On December 31. 1978, the Deputy Collector issued a notice under Rule 5(1)(b) of Rules, 1962 calling upon the respondent to submit their objections within 30 day from the time specified in the notice and also to appear before him on January 28, 1979 at 10.30 A.M. for hearing. The notice was served on the respondent on December 29, 1978 but he did not appear on that date. On March 31, 1979, the respondent filed an objection under Rule 6(3) of these Rules before the Deputy Commissioner, Raipur. The Deputy Collector overruled the objections and passed an order dated October 21, 1978 holding that the notice issued by the Deputy collector was valid and that the petitioner No. 2 was not entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right. On November 30, 1979 the Deputy Secretary to the Government of Madhya Bharat, Department of Home Affairs, Bhopal, issued a show cause notice under Section 4(2) of Act, 1962 on December 28, 1978 calling upon all the members of the respondent's family to submit objections and also objections in respect of the names of the petitioners. On January 29, 1980, the Assistant Collector passed an assessment order dated November 25. 1978 holding the petitioners guilty of the charge of failure to comply with Rule 6 (3) and (4) of Chapter 4 of the Madhya Bharat Rules, 1951. The petitioner No 2 filed an appeal against the said order before the Commissioner, Central Excise, Raipur, who by his order dated December 30, 1978 set aside the assessment order passed by the Assistant Commissioner on the ground that the petitioners were not entitled for the issue and objections to be heard before the revision was allowed. On February 28, 1980 the Deputy Director of Home Department, Raipur issued a fresh notice under sub-rule (1) Of Rule 5 of the said Rules calling upon each member of the petitioner to submit objection within 30 working days from that date and also file objections in the prescribed form within 30th day from that day. The petitioners filed their objections on February 28 and February 29, 1981 before the Assistant Director of the Home Department. On April 29, 1982 the Deputy Inspector General of Police, Raipur passed an interim order directing the respondent not to proceed with the revision. On May 31, 1983 the Deputy Superintendent of Police issued a final notice under Sub-rule 5 of Rule 5 on December 30. 1978 calling for objections and in pursuance thereof the petitioner filed his objection. The Assistant Director, Home Department by his proceedings dated October 25, 1979 rejected the objections filed by the respondent. On October 21. 1980 the respondent again filed an additional appeal against that order before a Division Bench of the High Court which was dismissed on November 30. 1981. On September 29, 1983, the petitioner moved this Court for special leave to appeal against this judgment and order. The petition was heard along with the main writ petition and by its order dated February 28. 1981 the High court allowed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 Rule 5 is not a rule of law or procedure prescribed for the purpose of holding that it is mandatory to hold an enquiry before passing any final order on the revision application. [475 D] 1.2 The High Court was in error in quashing the proceedings and setting aside the order of the Assistant Government dated October 30,1978. [441 G] 2.1 The High court has erred in holding that Rule 5 does not apply to the petitioner.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1947. The respondent, a director of the company, filed a return of his income for the assessment year 1954-55 on the ground that he had failed to file the balance sheet and profit and loss account before the general meeting held on December 31, 1956. The Income Tax Officer, who assessed the appellant's income at Rs. 1,000 per annum, found that the appellant was guilty of a breach of section 134 of the Act and accordingly issued a notice under section 143(1) of the said Act to the respondent. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The appellant filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue which was dismissed. The Board of revenue held that the provisions of sections 134 and 135 of the 1913 Act were not applicable to the case and accordingly directed the Income tax Officer to proceed with the assessment in accordance with law. On further appeal, the High Court of Orissa held that section 134(1)(c) of 1956 Act did not apply to the facts of this case and it was not open to the appellant to plead that the provision of sections 135 and 136 of the 1956 Act were applicable to him. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether on principle and authority it can be said that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134 or section 135 of 1956. Section 134(2) of that Act provides that if any person, who has failed to comply with a notice issued under sub section (1) or subsection (2) or sub section(3) of section 143 of the Old Companies Act or sub sections (1), (3) and (4) of Section 135 of that 1956 Act, has failed in his return of income for any year, he shall be liable to pay a penalty which may extend to one lakh rupees. The High Court held that on principle it was open to him to plead the case at the general meetings before the company in the general body meeting and that the requirement of section 135(2)(c), as it stood prior to its amendment by Act No. 1 of 1956, did not come into play. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The provisions of section 137 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 were applicable only to a case where the liability to file a return was incurred by the company under sub sections(1),(3), (4), (5) and sub section 4 of Section 134 of that Code. [775 H] (b) The fact that the requirements of section 136 of 1956 were not complied with, does not make any difference in the case of a company which has failed as required by section 137. [750 A] (c) The provision of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 was applicable to a proceeding under section 135 and not to a prosecution under section 136. [751 B] (d) The High court was wrong in holding that the proviso to sub section 2 of Section 137 of 1956 did not provide for any penalty or punishment for failure to file an account as required under section 138. [753 H] In the instant case, the appellant had failed in its return of the income for a period of two years from the date of the notice issued by the Income-tax Officer and therefore it was within his knowledge that he did not file the account as prescribed under section 137(2). [751 G] (e) The proviso to section 138 does not apply in the facts and circumstances of this appeal. [764 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1968. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the Orissa High Court in Misc. Case No. 14 of 1966. S. K. Bagga, for the appellant. M. C.

The appellant was a member of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, which was in force at the time when the Act was made. The State Government issued an order under section 5(1) of the Act directing that "the provisions of this Act shall apply to all persons or classes of persons or class of cases as the State Government may by general or special order direct". The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the Act did not provide for speedier trial and that it was not necessary to make any provision for the speediers trial. It further held that section 5 (1) was ultra vires the Constitution only so far as it permits the State government to direct any case to be tried by a Special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the proclamations. The appellant challenged the validity and correctness of the decision in this appeal on the ground that the provisions of section 5 were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The learned Judges held that there was no discrimination between the persons who had been tried by the Special Court and those who had not been tried before it, and that the classification made by the State legislature was not a reasonable classification in the interests of the public or the public interest. The appeal filed by the appellant against the decision of the High court was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) Section 5(2) of West Bengal Act is ultra vires and unconstitutional as it provides for speeder trial. [775 H] (b) The provisions of article 16 are not violative on any ground but they are in the nature of a safeguard against arbitrary or discriminatory treatment. [750 A] (c) The provision for speardness trial is not violative by reason of the fact that it requires speedieration to be made in the light of the object of the legislation as contained in article 14 and therefore the Special Courts had no jurisdiction to try these "cases" of the respondents. [751 B] (d) The Act does not provide any procedure for the sitting or hearing of these " cases". It only provides for the procedure which is prescribed by it. [751 D] (e) The object of section 3(2)(a), as it was enacted, was to provide for the first time that the Special courts shall have jurisdiction to hear all persons and classes of cases and matters connected with the speeders trial of certain offences. [764 G] (f) The Special Courts are not courts within the meaning of section 4(1)(b). [785 H] In the instant case, the Act does provide for a speediment trial. The provisions contained in section 5 are not in the interest of the general public or public interest and they do not require any special procedure. The Company was incorporated in the year 1947, and it had a capital of Rs. 1,50,000/- per annum. The Company was formed with effect from April 1, 1948, and its total number was fixed at Rs. 95. The total number of workmen employed by the Company was about Rs. 5,00,000/-. The Company paid to the workmen the minimum wages in respect of the Company's employees. On December 31, 1957, the Company made an application for fixation of minimum wage of Rs 1,25,000/per annum. In this application, it was alleged that the Company had not provided for any additional bonus at the rate of three months' basic wages and dearness allowance, and that the total number in respect thereof was about 2,50. The Tribunal rejected the claim on the ground that, under the Agreement of 1959, the workmen were entitled to minimum wages at the rates specified in the agreement. On appeal by the workmen, the High Court held that the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal was not a consolidated wage and that, therefore, there was no justification for introducing a new element of payment of bonus to the Company. The High Court further held that, as the Company did not provide for any extra wages at all, it could not be said that there was any justification to introduce a new elements of payment. In appeal by special leave, the appellant has contended that the Tribunal committed an error of law in holding that there is no justification to introduced a new component of payment to the workman and, therefore the Tribunal erred in rejecting this claim on that ground. The question whether the Company should be paid minimum wages or not was considered by this Court in [Union of India vs. Bombay Tyre International Ltd.] , and it was held that if the Company has provided for additional bonus to workmen, it is not open to the Tribunal to ignore the provisions of the Agreement and make an award on the basis of the said agreement. In the present case, the Tribunal did not consider the question whether there was a provision in the Agreement regarding the minimum rate of wages or that, according to the Award,, the total amount payable by the company was about two lakhs per annum and, accordingly, it rejected the contention raised on behalf of the workmen. The appellant has also contended that, in any event, the award is vitiated by error of fact. In support of this contention, the learned counsel for the appellant relied upon the decision of this Court reported in [Indian Oil Corporation Ltd., vs. Employees' State Insurance Corpn.] , referred to and relied upon.

Ramchand Jain, was an employee of the respondent-Bank and he was served with a notice of demand under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") on April 30, 1962, for payment of the amount due to him. He filed a petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter called "the Code") in the High court of Gujarat, Ahmedabad, praying that the proceedings before the Income -tax Officer were not maintainable and that the said proceedings are liable to be quashed on the ground that notice under [section 142(1)] of the Incometax Act was issued by him. The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The assessment proceedings were completed on March 28, 1939, and the Income tax Officer issued notice of demand for the period from April 13, 1938 to March 31, 1939. On March 30, 1939 the appellant filed an appeal against the order of assessment before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant commissioner allowed the appeal holding that there was a discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and that the income, profits and gains of the period between April 13 , 1938 and March 28 , 1939 were not the income of the appellant. On further appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the assessment was valid and that there could be no question of the discontinuance of business within section 25 (4) as it stood before its amendment in 1939. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 25(3) of Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 is a provision for the purpose of section 26(2). It provides that where any business or profession has paid tax under this Act in respect of any income, profit and gains arising from such business, profession or vocation, the change in the constitution of such business shall be deemed to have been the income. [605 G] 1.2 The High court was wrong in holding that the assessee was not liable to pay tax for the assessment year 1939-40. [650 D] 1:3 The question whether there was discontinuance of a business within Section 25 (1) or not, is a mixed question of law and fact and it cannot be decided by this Court in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution. [663 H] 1 Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the assessee is entitled to succeed in his appeal under section 26 (2) of The Income tax Appellate Tribunal Act, 1957, is not a question of fact but one of law. [664 D] 2.1 The High Courts have taken a contrary view and have held that there is no question that there has been a discontinuance or discontinuance of any business within s. 25(1). [663 F] 2:2 In the instant case, there was an discontinuance of some business within S. 25 (3) read with section 26 of the Act of 1918. There was no discontinuance of such a business and the income- profits were not liable for tax under section 25. The question in the present appeal is whether there has to be a discontinuance and if so, whether it can be said that there must be a succession only to the business which had paid tax in respect thereof under the Act. [662 G] 2] In the present case, as already stated, there is an discontinuance or discontinued of some of the businesses within Sect. 25 of the Incometax Act, 1961 and the question whether the income profits were the income from the business itself was a mixed issue of law or fact and not one of fact. [766 D] 3.1 In the circumstances, it cannot but be held that in the assessment proceedings for the year 1939, there has not been any discontinuance of that business within [section 25(2)] of the Indian Incometax Act. The appeal is allowed with costs.

The plaintiff 's father was a member of the joint family. He died in the year 1955 and his wife, the widow of the deceased, was entitled to 1/4th share in the property which she had inherited from her husband. The plaintiff 'S.R.D.A. was the owner of the property. On the death of the father, the plaintiff ' s right to claim partition was extinguished by the operation of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act. The trial court held that the plaintiff was entitled only to a 1/3rd share in his coparcenary property and not to a half share in that property. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. On further appeal, it was contended by the plaintiff that the partition between the plaintiff and her husband was effected on the basis of the provisions of section 18A(9) of the Act and as such the plaintiff could not be treated to have a 1⁄4th interest in the coparcenary property. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the share of the plaintiff in the joint Hindu family property was not allotted to him if he had received any partition during her husband's life time between him and his two sons. [675 H] (2) Section 6 of Hindu Successions Act provides that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener "shall be deemed to be the share in such property which would have been allotted to the deceased coparcener if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before her death". The mere fact that a partition had actually taken place between the parties does not by itself give rise to a right to a share in coparcenary property unless it is shown that a division has actually taken effect between the two sons of the same Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary. [775 H; 776 B] (3) Section 18A of the Indian Succession Act provides for a situation where a coparcener dies before his death and his interest in a coparcenary property is extinguished by operation of law. The mere circumstance that a coparcener has got 1/2 share in a joint family property does not give rise of a right of partition to a coparcener unless it be shown that such a partition took place immediately prior to his death. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1987. From the Judgment and Order dated 14.8.1987 of the Madras High Court in S.A.(O.S.)No.412 of 1986. V.N. Ganpuley, K.K. Venugopal, R.M. Sahai, M.V. Goswami, P.Krishnan, A.K Gupta and B.Rowella for the Appellant. Vrajlal G. Balakrishnan, S.Kathiresan, M/s. Vam Organic Co., and M.S. Kandasamy for the Respondents. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 14th August 1987 of the High court of Madras in SM.A(O.P.)No 1 of 1986 whereby the High Curt allowed the suit filed by the appellant and dismissed his suit.
