The father of the parties died during the pendency of the suit and his son, the appellant had 1/8th share therein. The High court held, as stated above, that the shares of the family property were not allotted in favour of the wife of the husband of the respondent. The question whether a partition has taken place on the date of the application for partition was considered by the High. Court and it was held that there is no need to go into the question of share of joint family properties.

The respondent was appointed as a Class III employee in the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Class II and Class III post on or before 1st October, 1956 and he was promoted as Class IV employee on or prior to 1st November, 1956 by virtue of a new sub regulation (2) of regulation 19. The respondent was promoted in the year 1965 as Class I employee on 1st December, 1966. He joined service after 1 st September, 1957. On his retirement he was appointed to the service of the Corporation by virtue o f the settlement dated 29th May, 1967. He had been promoted to a Class II post on 1 st October, 1959 and he continued in service till he attained the age of 60 years. The 1st Respondent was appointed in the service as Class III employees on or about 1st January, 1966 and he joined service on or around 31st December 1966. On the basis of the said appointment he was reverted to his original post by virtue thereof. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to continue in service beyond the age o 60 years as he had been appointed to Class III posts on or wo uld be raised to 60 years and, therefore, he could not be reverted to the original post. On a consideration of the provisions of regulation 20(2) and the proviso thereto it was held that since the respondent had been reverted to Class I post by way of punishment, he was entitled to be reinstated in service on completion of 58 years of age. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court against the said decision. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order passed by the High court is correct and there is no merit in the appeal. [557 G] 1.2 The respondent had joined service as a class III employee on the date he attained 60 years of the age. He could not have been reverted without following the procedure prescribed under regulation 19(2). [558 H] 1:3. The order of the High Curt is correct. [506 A] 1 Whether the respondent has been promoted in accordance with the said regulations or not, can be decided only after the expiry of the period of service as provided in regulation 20. [504 B] 2.1 There was no provision for reversion of employees who had joined the service prior to the date of the order dated 29 th May, 1968. The proviso to regulation 19 (2), however, did not apply to the respondent.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab National Bank. He was elected as Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank in the year 1962. The respondent filed an application before the High Court for permission to withdraw his resignation from the office of Chairman of Punjab National bank. The High Court allowed the said application and permitted the withdrawal of the resignation. On appeal by the State, the Division Bench reversed the order passed by the High court and held that the letter dated December 10, 1962 was not a contempt of court. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High.Court fell into error in holding that the appellants committed contempt of Court. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the letters were not a matter of any kind but were merely an administrative order and did not constitute contempt. It was further urged that the resignation letter dated January 10, 1963 was not an act of contempt. In support of this contention, the learned counsel relied upon the decision of this Court in [State of Punjab vs. Amar Singh] ; , referred to. The Division Bench held that a mere change of opinion or a change of the opinion of the High Courts is not sufficient to constitute contempt and accordingly dismissed the application. It is contended by the appellant's counsel that the respondent was guilty of contempt of the court. The question whether the appellants were guilty of any contempt of a court has to be decided on facts in each case. In the absence of such a finding, the High' Court should not have accepted the apology tendered by the appellants. It may be noted that the Division bench held that there was no contempt of itself and the appellants had committed contempt. The Bench also held that if the appellants committing any contempt, the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether any person did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter could have been ascertained by court on fact whether any other Judge did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court and that the question of contempt was a disputed question of fact. In view of this finding, it was held that no question arises for acceptance of apology. The appellant's advocate also submitted that in view of the decision in Amar Singh's case (supra) the Division Benches fell into the error of accepting the apology. In our opinion, the appeal is without merit and should be dismissed.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee, a resident of Bombay, was an individual and a Hindu Undivided Family. He was assessed as an individual on his behalf. On appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, he upheld the order of assessment. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it held that section 5(1) of the impugned Act violated the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution and was void and unenforceable. The Tribunal held that the assessee had evaded payment of tax under section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. On further appeal by special leave, the High Court held that in view of the decision of this Court in [Commissioner of Income Tax vs. M/s. [M/s] [Metal Box Company Ltd.] , the assessment was bad and not according to law. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of section 5 (1) read with section 5 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 6(5) of Act did not violate article 14 or 19 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 4(4)(a) of Indian Income Tax Act, which is a special provision in respect of escaped income and which provides for imposition of penalty under section 5A of the said Act, was void as offending against article 14 and 19 of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 6 (5) are not applicable to cases where the assessee has evaded payment by reason of the failure of the assessee to make a full and true disclosure of his income or the failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment under section 4 of the Income tax. [605 H] 2. The expression "reasonably" in section 5 is not defined in the Act and it has been held by this Court that section 3(4) of that Act does not violate any article of the petitioner's Constitution. [650 A] 3. Section 6 (1)(a), as amended, is a provision which provides that where an assessee has concealed his income, he shall be liable to penalty under sub section (4) and sub section 4A of section 8 of the Central Act. [663 H] 4. The words "reasonly" in clause (b) of section 34 are not defined either in the Indian income tax Act or in the Income Tax law. [664 D] 5. Section 5(2) of this Act does provide for imposition and assessment of penalty on an assessee under section 6 of the Incometax Act. It is true that section 8(1)(c) provides for imposing a penalty under clause (a) but it does not make any difference whether the assessee was a resident or not. [665 F] 6. The word "reason" in sub section 2 of section 4 is not restricted to any other ground and it cannot be used to describe the grounds on which an order of reassessment can be made. [666 D] 7. Section 8(2)(b) does not infringe article 14, because it provides for a penalty. It only provides that if the assessee fails to make full and correct disclosure of income or loss in any material particulars necessary for assessment under sub sections (1), (4A) and (4B) of s. 5A, he is liable to be proceeded against under section 8. [667 G] 8. The language of section 9(2), as it stood before the amendment of section 24(3) of Finance Act, 1987, shows that the expression " reason" in the said section does not include any other reason. [668 A] 9.

The Federation is a registered society. The respondent was a member of the Federation. He was a registered Society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. He had been elected as a member to the membership of the said Society. On his election he was declared elected by the members of the Association. The appellant filed an application before the High Court for a writ of mandamus directing the respondent to declare him as a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(j) of the Act. The High Court held that the respondent was not a " commercial establishment" and, therefore, he was not entitled to be declared as a 'shop' under section 2 (1)(d) of that Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The expression "commercial" in section 2 is wide enough to include within it all the property and income of the association which includes the idea of profit. It is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the respondent is a "Commercial Establishment" or not. The expression 'commercial establishment' has been defined in section 3(1) of Act, which reads as follows: "3(1). " commercial Establishment" means any establishment, including an association of individuals, a trade, business, undertaking, manufacture, occupation, trade, calling or employment, whether such establishment is engaged in the business of manufacturing, supplying or distributing goods, or in rendering services, whether by way of sale, purchase, lease, assignment or otherwise." (ii) The term "commercial Establishment" has been used in section 4(1)(b) of this Act. It reads as under: "4.(1). 'Commercial Establishment' means any premises including an establishment which is a commercial establishment. (2) In this section, the expression "industrial establishment" includes any establishment including an Association of individuals and industrialists, but does not include any association of persons or any other society."

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that he was entitled to a share of the income from agricultural lands in the assessment year 1837-1837 and that the income derived by him from the land was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that the allowance was not a revenue receipt but an amount which was received as a consideration for the transfer of the interest in the land and, therefore, it was exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of that Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. The Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled only to a sum of money equivalent to the income received by him as a result of the transfer and not to a portion of the amount which he had received as consideration for his transfer. In further appeal to this Court, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal erred in holding that the amount received by the assessee as a receipt was agricultural income and not an income from land. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in its view that the deduction under section 2 (1)(b) of Act was not revenue expenditure but an allowance made in lieu of any beneficial interest in land. [675 H] 2. The amount received as compensation by the appellant as a consequence of transfer of his interest in agricultural lands is not agricultural receipt and, consequently, it cannot be held to be exempt from tax under section 5(1) (a) or (b). [682 B] 3. Section 4(2)(i), which provides that the Income Tax Officer shall not be entitled to receive any amount by way of compensation in respect of any land or part thereof in excess of the ceiling limit, does not apply to a case where a portion is received as income from agriculture and the income is exempt from payment of tax under [section 4(1)] (a). [650 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th July, 1971 of the Allahabad High Court in Misc. Case No. 12/70. S. K. Sinha and P. C. Agarwala for the Appellant. M. C.. Mathur and Ravinder Narain for Respondent No. 1. B. Sen, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for Respondent Nos. 2 to 4. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal is directed against a judgment of the High Court of Allahabad dated October 10, 1971 in Misc Case No 12/ 70. The appellant is a Hindu Undivided Family. He filed an application under section 7 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for the assessment years 1837 and 1838-1839. The respondent was assessed by the Income-tax Officer under the provisions of the [Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1952] (Act No. 27 of 1952). The appellant claimed that his income from the agricultural lands was exempt under section 3(2) of this Act. He also claimed that the said income was not liable to be included in the total income of the family. The claim was rejected by the Assistant Commissioner and the order was confirmed by the Appellate Authority. The appeal filed by the respondent before the Income -tax Appellate Tribunal was allowed on the basis that the appellant was entitled for a sum equivalent to his share in the agricultural land. The Appellate Tribunal held, relying upon the decision of this Court in [Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Sri Krishna Gopal] , referred the question of law arising out of the order passed by the High court in Misc case No.12/70 and answered that question in favour of the respondent.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Foreman in the year 1964 and they were promoted to the post of Chargeman II on ad hoc basis. They were confirmed in the post o f the post on completion of two years' service as Supervisor 'A'. On their appointment they were given promotion to the higher post with effect from the date their junior was promoted. The appellants filed a writ petition before the Madhya Pradesh High Court which was dismissed by order dated 2nd February, 1981. Thereafter, the appellants filed an appeal before this Court in 1983 and the same was allowed by order of this Court dated 4th April, 1983. In the meantime, the respondents were promoted as Chargeman I on ad-hoc basis with effect fr om the date they were appointed to the said post. The State Government issued a notification dated 28th December, 1965 under which the appellants were promoted in the grade of Chargemen II on completion o f two years service as Supervisors 'A' and were given the benefits of promotion to all such of the petitioners before the said date. On or about 2nd March, 1981, the State Government passed an order dated 16th April 1983 under which they were granted promotion to Grade I with effect fro m the date of their appointment. The respondents filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and also praying for a direction to the appellants to give them the benefits as were given by the Madhya Prade sh High Court to such of those petitioners before that Court wo uld be granted the same benefits as was given to the other petitioners before th e said date, and also to grant consequential reliefs. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the respondents in limine on the ground that the appellants had not challenged the validity o f their promotion order dated 29th December 1965. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was wrong in holding that the said orders were passed without giving an opportunity of hearing to the respondents before passing the impugned order and, therefore, they should be given the same benefit as was granted to the others before that date. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated 30th December 1966 is not a speaking order but it is a speaking one. [457D] 2. The question whether the appellants have been promoted to Grade II with effect o f promotion or not is a matter of policy decision of the Government and the Court cannot sit in appeal over such decisions unless they are shown to be vitiated by mala fides or bias. [557F] 3. The fact that the respondents had been given proper place in the gradation list does not mean that the same treatment should have been given to them before the date on which they had been promoted. [506D] 4. The Government was right in holding the appellants as Chargemen- II with retrospective effect from 1st April, 1979 and they cannot be denied the benefit of promotion merely because they were entitled to be treated as Charge Man I. [504F] 5. The decision of this court in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [54E] 6. The respondent was promoted as a Chargeman-II on ad hoe basis with retrospective date from 1 st April, 1978 and he was given promotion as Charge man I on regular basis with prospective effect from that date and was given the benefit thereof. [55G] 7. The said decision is not attracted to the present facts of this case. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellants, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and the private operators of the transport undertaking were granted permits for the period from 1.4.1971 to 31.3.1972. The said period was extended by a notification issued under section 63(7) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The appellants filed applications for grant of stage carriage permit in respect of their tourist vehicles on the ground that they were entitled to ply in the State Transport Undertaking for operating in any inter State route. The application was rejected by the Regional Transport Authority and the High Court held that the permits granted to the private operator were valid. The appellants challenged the order of the Regional transport authority before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The scheme of the Act is not violative of article 14 of the Constitution. [655 H] 1.2 The scheme for grant and renewal of permits is a policy decision of the State Government and the same cannot be challenged on the grounds that the said policy was arbitrary or unreasonable. The object of the scheme is to provide for the grant of permits in respect to inter State routes, and so to interpret the word 'preference' occurring in section 63 (7) as well as to be given to the "such operators of tourist cars, or such travel agents, as may be approved in this behalf by the Ministry dealing in tourism. [650 H] 2.1 There is no substance in the contention that the scheme of grant and the renewal of permit are not violative on any ground. The scheme is not discriminatory and it is not open to the appellants to challenge the validity of the schemes. [663 A] 1:2 The object behind the scheme was to provide a monopoly in favour of the private transport operators, and the object was to ensure that the conditions imposed by the State Road transport Corporation were fulfilled. [664 D] 2:3 The scheme was not violative either of article14 or Article 14 of Constitution. The policy decision taken by the Government is not arbitrary or irrational. The question whether the permits are valid or not is a matter for the State to decide and it cannot be questioned on the basis that the policy decision is arbitrary or discriminatory. [662 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th May, 1971 of the Karnataka High Court in Writ Petition No. 8 of 1970. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellants. M. C. Bhandare, K. Rajendra Chowdhary and P. H. Parekh for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 9, 1971 passed by the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal in Writ Appeal No 15 of 1971. The appellant-Karnataka State RoadTransport Corporation Ltd., has filed this appeal by special leave against the order dated September 10, 1970 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Karnataka in Writ petition No.8 of 1970 and the writ petition was dismissed on the short ground that the appellants were not challenging the validity or the policy decisions taken by them. The facts giving rise to the present appeal are as follows: The appellants are the transport operators operating in the notified routes. They have obtained permits for plying in the said route. On their application, the Regional Manager of the Central Government, Bangalore, made an order on September 10. 1970, rejecting the applications filed by the appellants for grant or renewal of a stage carriage permits. The Regional Transport Officer rejected the applications for the reasons that the applications were not maintainable. The appeals were dismissed by the High. Court and the Writ Petition was allowed. Hence these appeals. The only question which arises in this appeal is whether the permit granted to private operators in respect o State transport undertaking from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation Ltd. to the State Trading Corporation of India Ltd., is valid or otherwise.

The respondent was a registered dealer in the State of Madras. He purchased a business premises at Madras and sold it to the respondent on October 5, 1956. The respondent paid sales tax under the Act on the basis that he had purchased the business premises from the State Government. On October 6, 1956, the respondent filed an application for registration of his business under section 19(1) of the Act before the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Madras. The said application was rejected by the Assistant Collector of Commercial Tax, Madras, on the ground that the respondent did not pay sales tax in respect of the turnover of the sale of the business. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the sales effected by the respondent were liable to be taxed under section 10(2) (c) of Act No. IX of 1939 and accordingly the respondent was entitled to a refund of the amount paid by him. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the sale effected by him was not liable to tax under section 9(1)(b) of Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. On further appeal, Held: (i) Section 10(1), as it stood before the amendment of 1956, did not apply to a case where the business was transferred to the State and was therefore governed by section 19 of the said Act. The words "in respect of" in section 9 of the Madras General sales Tax Act were wide enough to include within its scope the power of the State to levy tax on the sale or purchase of goods, as the case may be. (ii) Section 19(2)(c) did not operate retrospectively and it was not open to the Government to make a new assessment under section 11 of the Tamil Nadu General Sales tax Act, 1958. [775 H] The respondent was liable to pay sales-tax on the turnover in respect thereof as he had not paid any sales tax. The question whether the sale was liable for payment of sales tax did not arise at all in view of the amendment made by section 8 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956 and the amended provision was ultra vires of the rule making power of State Government under section 3 of the Central Sales Tax (Second Amendment) Act. [750 H] In the present case, the assessee had purchased a new business premises in which the business of the assessee was being carried on and the transfer of the same was not covered by the said provision. The sale effected in the course of the transaction was liable under section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act. Under section 19 (2) of that Act, the tax assessed on the transferee is to be paid in accordance with the provisions of the section. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 979 of 1972. From the Judgment and Order dated the 30th September, 1970 of the High Court of Madras in Writ Petition No. 1124 of 1970. S. T. Desai, V. M. Tarkunde, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. K.K. Venugopal, S. Balakrishnan, Sridharan Nair and P. Ram Reddy for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, C.J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 30, 1970 passed by the High court of Madras dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant. The appellant is a registered firm carrying on business at Madras. It has been assessed to tax in accordance With section 9 (1) (b) read with section 19 and section 5 (2)(a) of Central Sales tax (Amendment Act, 1957). The respondent is a dealer in goods, who purchased the said business premises for the purpose of carrying on the business as a dealer. On September 6, 1959, the appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of assessment and the said appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Authority.

The appellant, a public servant, was appointed as a Civil Assistant Surgeon in the State of Bombay on January 1, 1954. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Superintendent of Police and was posted at the Police Training College, Bombay. On March 31, 1955, he was transferred to the State Government of Bombay. The State Government issued an order dated April 30, 1956, under section 60(2)(a) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, transferring him to the Central Government. He challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay which was dismissed on May 29, 1957. On June 27, 1958, the appellant filed a writ application in the Bombay High Court challenging the validity and correctness of the order passed by the State government. The High Court allowed the writ application holding that the order dated March 31,. 1956, was not a decree within section 60 (2)(b) of that Act and that the decree passed by it was not an award within section 61(1) of Bombay Reorganisation act, 1960. On behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the High court erred in holding that there was no contract between the State and the appellant and that as the order of transfer was not one under section 61 (2), the decree could not be sustained. The learned Single Judge held that the transfer of the respondent to the Government of Maharashtra was a decree for payment of arrears of salary and it was therefore not a nullity. On appeal, the Division Bench reversed the judgment of the learned Single judge and allowed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed on April 30,. 1956 by the Government is not an order in writing but an order made by the Central government under section60(2) of this Act. [605 H] 2.1 The order dated May 29. 1957 was a judgment within section 62 of the Indian States Reorganisation Act. 1960, and therefore it could not have been passed by that authority. [706 C] 2:2 It is true that there may be an agreement between the Government and the State in which the respondent was appointed to serve as a civil Assistant Surgeon for the period from January 1,. 1956 to March 31. 1955, but that does not mean that the said agreement could have been executed by the appellant. [700 D] 2(i) The order of the State Govt. dated April 29, 1956 was not in writing and therefore the decree was not executable. [750 E] (ii) The decree passed on May 30, 1957, was a nullity because it was an award. [800 G] 2.(iii) The judgment of this Court in the case of [Western India Tripura vs State of Tripura] , referred to. 3.1 It is well settled that a decree can be executed by a civil court only if the order under section 62(2), as amended, was an order passed in writing. [805 H; 806 A] 2 (iv) The High court was right in holding, relying on the judgment in the said case, that there is no contract in existence between the appellant as a public officer and the Government. [907 G] 3.2 It cannot be said that there has been any agreement between a State and a person who is appointed to be a civil assistant Surgeon for a period of one year or until he attains the age of superannuation, whichever is earlier. The judgment in that case was not based on any such agreement. [900 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1966. The appellant was the owner of a land measuring about 3 acres and 10 gunthas situated in village Kokari, District Kanpur. The respondents filed an application under section 6 of the Indian Mines Act for permission to remove coal from the encroached area. The Deputy Commissioner of Kanpur, who had jurisdiction over the area, held that the respondents were entitled to remove the coal from their land. On appeal by the appellant, the Additional Collector, Kanpur, allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner. In an appeal filed by the respondents, the High Court held that under the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946 the right of the appellant to remove any coal was not lost to them for ever. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 6(1) of the Act the respondents could not claim exemption from the operation of rule 76 of the said rules. On a reference made by the High court, the following question was referred to the High, Court: "Whether the right to remove or remove coal under the provisions contained in the Indian Mining Act and the Rules framed thereunder the appellants are entitled to use the land for any purpose other than that mentioned in the Schedule of the rules?". The High court answered the question in favour of the respondents. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the right conferred upon the appellant under section 3(1)(b) of Indian Mines Regulation Act and Rule 76 of Indian Coal Mining Regulation, were not lost or destroyed by being rendered infructuous. The contention was accepted by the Court. The question whether the respondents had knowledge of the coal removed from the land was decided in favour by the trial court. In the appeal to this Court it was submitted that under section 5(1), the right which the appellant had acquired was not a matter of statutory obligation on the part of the plain. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right conferred by section 3 (1)(a) of Act and rule 76 are in the nature of a "stamp" or "street". [675 H] 2. Section 6(2) of India Mines Regulation provides that no person shall use any land for carrying on any mining operation except under the authority and subject to the provisions, if any, of the Mines Act and Rules made thereunder. The words "and" are not defined in the Act or in the rules framed thereunder. [682 H] 3. Section 5(2)(b), as it stood before the amendment by Act No. XI of 1947, provided that no right to use any property for carrying out any mining operations except under a licence granted under section 4 of the Central Act and rules made thereunder shall be transferred or otherwise dealt with in respect of such area. [650 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal Nos. 1523-1524 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1976 of the Allahabad High Court in C.M.W. No. 814 of 1975. S.K. Dhingra, V.C. Mahajan, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. M.S. K. Sastri, D. N. Mukherjee, P.K Gupta and A.K Jain for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. These appeals are directed against a common judgment dated September 9, 1976 passed by a Division Bench of the High Courts of Allahabad and Allahabad. The facts leading to these appeals are as follows: The appellant is a company registered under the Companies Act and has its factory at Kanpur. It had leased out the land in question to the respondent for a period of five years from the date of the lease. On the expiry of the period of lease, the respondent was entitled to continue to use and enjoy the land as a lessee till the expiry or termination of the tenancy.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an employee of the respondent. The respondent was employed as a clerk in the appellant's office at Bombay. He was dismissed from service on January 8, 1957. On December 9, 1958, he filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 1,000/- and Rs. 2,500/- respectively with interest at the rate of 18% per annum. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was guilty of misconduct and therefore the action taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing orders was not bona fide and was not colourable exercise of power. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the order terminating the services of the appellant was a colourable exercise or an unfair labour practice and it was not a colourable act on the part of the employer. The appellant's appeal to this Court was dismissed. It is contended for the appellant that the tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether there was misconduct and if so, whether the action was bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practices. In support of this contention reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in [The State of Bombay vs The United Motors (India) Ltd.] , referred to above. It was held that in order to satisfy the tribunal that there was in fact misconduct and it is not a case where the action has been taken under the Standing Orders, it must be shown that there is in fact an unfair Labour practice and the action is bona fide. In this case the tribunal found that the action of the management was bona fides and was a mere colourable exercise. The High Court further held that even if the order was passed by the tribunal it was a nullity. It may be mentioned that the appellant had not challenged the validity of the order before the tribunal but it is clear from the order that the question as to whether there has been misconduct or not was raised and decided in the earlier proceedings. The tribunal also held that there were no grounds for interfering with the order passed by an Industrial Court relating to termination of service under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. In our opinion, therefore, the appellant is right in contending that the decision in the present case does not apply to the facts of this case because that was a pure question of fact and it cannot be said that the view taken by industrial courts in this regard is a perverse order. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in the city of Bombay. He filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he had become the owner of the property by virtue of an agreement dated December 1, 1960. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenancy was not terminated by the landlord and that the respondent was entitled to recover possession of the building from the appellant. On appeal the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the agreement dated November 27, 1960, created a lease and that in view of the provisions of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act, the respondent could not be said to have become the tenant of the premises by virtue thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that in terms of an oral agreement dated March 27, 1954, the tenancy had been terminated by a written notice and that it was open to the landlord to terminate the tenancy by giving notice in writing to the tenant. [775 H] 2.1 The question whether the agreement was a lease or not is a matter which can be decided only at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, the Court has no jurisdiction to go into that question. [750 A] 2:2 In the instant case, the agreement of December 1 1960, was created by the respondent in favour of the respondent. The agreement dated January 27, 1959, created an oral tenancy and that document of November 27 1960, executed by the appellant in favour the respondent, was a deed of lease. [751 B] 2(i) The question as to whether the relationship between the parties had been established or not was a matter for determination of the Court and it was not decided in that behalf. [751 H] (ii) The agreement of November 28 1960, which created an agreement of tenancy, was one of lease and not a lease. It was only a document of the nature of a lease that could be said under section 28(2) of the Act. [764 G] 2.(iii) The High court was right when it held that the appellant had become owner of property by operation of law. [754 H] 3.1 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the relationship of the parties was such as could be decided in the suit and the respondent had not been able to establish his rights in the premises. The question of tenancy being a matter between the appellant and the landlord does not arise at all. [752 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1134 of 1972. Dhebar, for respondent No. 1 (in all the appeals) The Judgment of the court was delivered by RAY, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment dated October 10, 1972 passed by a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court in First Appeals Nos. 15 of 1972 and 16 of 1971 whereby the High Courts' decision in Second Appeals Nos.. 15/72 and 16/72 were reversed. The appellant is a tenant under the respondent who was inducted as a tenant on December 1. 1960. He had been paying rent for the period from December 1 to December 31, 1961. On March 27. 1959, he filed an application before the trial Court for eviction of the tenant on the grounds set out in the plaint. The respondent contested the suit by filing written statement and contended that the suit was not maintainable as it was barred by time.

The petitioner was appointed as a Constable in the Police Department on 29.3.1985 and he was confirmed in that post on 30th of August, 1985. He was given a temporary appointment by the Governor on 10.7.1986. The respondent was appointed to the post of Constable on 29th of July, 1985 and he joined duty on 30.8.1985. On his joining the service, he was promoted as Head Constable in December, 1986. Thereafter, he filed a Writ Petition before the High Court of Allahabad challenging the order dated 10.07.1986 passed by the Government of Uttar Pradesh rejecting the claim of the respondent for reinstatement in service. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of termination on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to continue in service beyond 30th August, 1986 as he had completed 58 years of age. The State filed an appeal against the judgment dated 24.3,1988 passed by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court which was dismissed by this Court on 24.03.1988. Thereafter the respondent filed a Review Petition before this Court claiming to be reinstated in service with full back wages and continuity of service. This Court allowed that Review Petition holding that the order passed by Government of U.P. dismissing the Writ Petition was not in accordance with law. The appellant filed a review petition which was also dismissed on 24th March, 1988. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 The respondent had been appointed as Constable in Police Department in December 1986 and he continued to work till 30th September, 1985 when he was appointed on 29-3-1985. He did not make any order on review of his appointment. [505D] 1.2 The High court has rightly held that the interim order dated 25.03.'1988 passed in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1986 was in accordance to law and therefore, the respondent should be treated as a person regularly appointed from 29th July,1985. [605E] 2.1 There is no merit in this appeal and it is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was a member of the police force. He was arrested on September 10, 1972 and was remanded to judicial custody till August 31, 1973. The case was registered against him under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. On October 30, 1973 he was arrested and produced before the Magistrate on the same day. The appellant was arrested in connection with a case which was registered as Crime No. 8 of 1973 under Section 307 read with Sections 34 and 34 IPC and was released on bail by the learned Sessions Judge. On September 16, 1973 the appellant filed an application for bail before the High Court. The High Court rejected the said application on the ground that the appellant had no motive to kill the deceased and that he was in a position to give his brotherhood and that the case was one based on circumstantial evidence. The learned Sessions judge held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed murder of the deceased. On appeal by the State, the High court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant under Section 304 Part I IPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The State filed an appeal against the said order before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to establish that the deceased was in any way responsible for the murder of his wife. [775 H] 2. The evidence on record shows that the occurrence took place at about 10 p.m. and the appellant was in the custody of the Police. The fact that he had been arrested in the presence of the Magistrate does not mean that he should have been in a fit state of mind to give creditworthy evidence for slender reasons. [750 H] 3. The question whether the accused committed murder or not is a matter which can be decided only by the Court and not by the High Courts. [751 G] 4. The facts on record show that the circumstances established beyond reasonable doubt, the possibility of the appellant committing murder of deceased cannot be ruled out. [751 H] 5. The mere fact that the evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable is not a ground to interfere with the order passed by the Sessions Judge and it is for the High Curt to consider whether the view taken by the trial court is reasonable or not. If the view of the trial Court is reasonable, the same should be upheld. [761 H; 771 A] 6. The provisions of Section 34 are mandatory in nature and they do not require that the conviction must be recorded on the basis of circumstantial evidence and it would be open to a court to interfere in the interest of justice. [771 D] 7. The accused has no motive or any other ground to commit murder of a person. [754 A] 8. The presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act is not applicable to the facts of the case. [752 B] 9. The burden of proving that the offence was committed by the appellant lies on him and he must prove that he has committed the offence. [758 G] 10. The position in law is well settled that the presumption under Sections 114 and 114 of Evidence Act, 1872 can be raised only when the evidence is clear and cogent. [759 D] 11. The decision of this Court in [State of U.P. vs Ram Singh] , referred to by the counsel for the appellant does not lay down correct law. [761 H] 12. The view taken in the case of State of Utter Pradesh vs Ram Kumar, is a possible view and it cannot be accepted.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court of India. He was appointed as a Judge in the State Judicial Service of the Union of India on January 1, 1962. On March 31, 1963 he was promoted to the post of District and Sessions Judge. On April 30, 1963, he was transferred to the High Court of Delhi. On May 29, 1963 the appellant filed an application before the Chief Justice of India for sanction under Section 6(1)(c) of the Act for prosecution of a person holding an office of profit under the Government of India or the State Government of any other State. The Chief Justice rejected the said application on the ground that the provisions of Article 124(4) were not applicable to the case and he was, therefore, not competent to sanction the prosecution of the appellant. On June 30, 1964, the appellant moved the High court for a writ quashing the order dated May 29. 1963 passed by the Chief Judge of Delhi and praying for a direction that the said order be quashed. The High Court dismissed the petition on July 14, 1965. On August 4, 1966, the President of India issued an order under Section 7(1) (c) directing the appellant to show cause why he should not be prosecuted for the offence punishable under section 5(1), 6(2) and 6(3) of Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court on August 4. 1966, praying that the High Courts of Delhi, Bombay and Calcutta, should issue a writ in the nature of certiorari quashing the orders dated May 30,1963 and June 30 1968 passed by them. On September 14, 1967, the High. Court dismissed his petition holding that the appellant was not competent for prosecution under Section 5(2). The appellant then filed a special leave petition against the said judgment before this Court. This Court held that the power of the Chief justice to impose any punishment on a Judge is a clear pointer in the direction that he must be removed from office in the manner provided in Article 124 (4) as well as Article 124 of the Constitution. The question whether the provisions contained in Article 217(2)(b) are applicable to cases where the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office was not considered by this Court and it was held that in such a case, the power under Article 217 could be exercised only if the alleged misconduct was connected with the office of the Judge. The Court observed that the question whether a person is competent for trial or punishment on the charge of corruption against a superior Judge was a matter which was not before this court and it would have been open to the appellant in the circumstances of the case to contend that the provision contained in Section 6 (1) of 1952 Act was applicable to him. The said decision was followed by this court in [State of West Bengal vs Union of Indian] . ; , referred to.

The appellant was a member of the Sunri caste. He was a Hindu by birth. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant to be set aside on the ground that he was a 'Hindu' within the meaning of s. 2(1)(d) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the appellant belonged to a larger caste group and, therefore, was excluded from the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 for the purpose of the said Sunri. The High Court also held that as the appellant had not been able to prove that he belonged to the 'tribe' which was included in item 42, the Tribunal should have set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the election petition to be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the respondent had not established that he belongs to a smaller caste group of Sahas. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant belonged not to a small caste but to a 'tribes' and, as such, was not entitled to be declared elected. [775 H] 2. The word 'castes' in item No. 40 is used in the sense of a person belonging to a particular caste or group of persons specified in items 40 and 41. Therefore, the appellant could not be said to belong to a different class apart from Sunri by caste. [750 A] 3. The expression 'tribals' in Item 40 includes 'cribes'. [750 B] 4. The words "including" in item 39 include 'c tribes". [750 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 15 of 1965. Appeal from the judgment and order dated September 30, 1964 of the Gujarat High Court in Election Petition No. 1 of 1964. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and R. Hathi for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated September 29, 1964 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Election petition No. 2 of 1964 filed by the appellant challenging his election to be void on the grounds that he has not established a case for the trial of the petition. The facts leading up to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was elected as a member from Sunitpur constituency. He challenged his election on the allegation that he had not proved that he belong to the Scheduled caste which was specified in Item No. 39 of Schedule I. The learned Judge held that there was no evidence to show that he belonging to the said Scheduled Caste which was a Scheduled Tribe within the definition of 'Scheduled Castes' in s.2(1) (d) and (e) of Act No. XLV of 1964, as amended by Act No, 1 of 1965, and that the High court was right in holding so. The appeal is accordingly allowed with costs.

The appellant was a tenant of the flat in which he had been residing at Bombay. He was given a monthly rent of Rs. 1,000 by the respondent. The appellant paid to the respondent a sum of Rs, 29,500 as rent for the flat and also a sum o f Rs. 2,000 on account of the cost of the car. On the appellant paying the amount of Rs,. 29, 500, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant in the Court of the Civil Judge, Bombay, for recovery of possession of the said flat. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the appellant to pay the sum of money as agreed between the parties. The respondent preferred an appeal before the District Court, which was allowed by the Additional District Judge, who set aside the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. On further appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the plaintiff's suit. In this Court it was contended that the appellant had not paid the amount as agreed to between the respondent and the appellant and that he was entitled to a decree for possession of flat in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was not entitled to the decree for recovery. [775 H] (2) The word "relinquish" used in the Transfer of Property Act is not defined in the Act and it has been used in a comprehensive sense. It means 'to do an act' as well as 'to give up possession of premises'. Therefore, the appellant was entitled only to a sum or consideration for the relinquishment of his tenancy. [750 H] The word 'relinquishes' is not a term of art and it includes within its ambit the word 'transfer' which is used in section 108, sub clause (i), of the Trans fer of Property. [751 A] (3) The words "on" and "surrender" are not defined either in the Indian Contract Act or in the Code of Civil Procedure. [75 H; 75 B] (4) The expression 'transfer of property' is used only in a broad sense and it does not include within its scope the transfer by a tenant to the landlord who receives any fine, premium or other like sum or deposit or any consideration for grant, renewal or continuance or the accord of consent on the ground that has been made an offence. [76 H] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 8 of 1977. Sharma for the Appellant. M. C. Bhandare, K. Rajendra Chowdhary and P. H. Parekh for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J.-This appeal is directed against a judgment dated March 3, 1976 passed by a Division Bench of the High court of Bombay in Criminal Appeal Nos. 8/75 and 9/75. The appellants were convicted under section 13(1)(d) read with section 108 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs., 500 each and in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one month. They were also directed to pay fine of rupees five thousand, in default of which they were ordered to undergo further rigorous imprisonment of six months. The High court confirmed their conviction and sentence under section 138 read with Section 108 of that Code. The State of Bombay has filed this appeal against the judgment dated 3rd March, 1976. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was working as a Manager in the Bank of Baroda at Bombay and he had taken a loan from the respondent for a sum Rs. 5,000/- on the security of his property.

The respondent, a contractor, filed an application under Section 33-C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") before the Tribunal for revision of wage scales. The Tribunal held that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the revised wage scale and directed the appellant to pay to each individual workman a sum of Rs. 150/and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. It also directed that the amount of Rs, 100/and odd should be paid to each of the employees in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 50/and the remaining amount of the workmen in the categories of Draftsman and Rs., 100/respectively. The respondent challenged the order of the Tribunal by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to revise the wage scales as it was not clearly mentioned in the award, and directed that an all round flat increase of Rs 150/ should be made to the workmen concerned. It further held that a flat increase in the scale of pay should be given to each workman who belonged to the Union staff, the financial condition of which was such that it would have to be paid at least to those employees who were entitled to receive the same amount of pay as they had been receiving from the Union. The appellant filed an appeal against this order before the Supreme Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was wrong in holding that a Flat increase in scale of Rs 100/was not justified. [775 H] 1.2 In the case at hand, the respondent had been paid a sum equivalent to the amount which he had received from the union staff. It is true that the Industrial Tribunal did not give any specific finding on this point but it was also wrong in saying that an All-India Industrial Disputes Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the dispute between the parties. [750 H] 2.1 There is no merit in the contention of the respondent that a sum equal to the pay which he was receiving from his union should be added to the basic pay and dearness allowance payable to him. The award passed by the Tribunal was erroneous. [751 G] 2:2 In view of the finding recorded by the Industrial Court, it is not open to the appellant now to contend that an additional amount of a flat rate should be granted to each employee who belonged either to the union or to any other workman. [751 H] 3.1 It was not open for the respondent to contend before the Industrial court that an employee should have been paid at the rate of Rs 50/per month as he had been deprived of the benefit under the Act. The Industrial Tribunal was wrong. [752 G] 3:3 The award is erroneous and it is liable to be set aside. [761 H; 754 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1977. From the Judgment and Order dated the 10th September, 1976 of the High court of Delhi in C.W.P. No. 1123 of 1978. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagga, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma for the Appellant. M.C. Bhandare, Ms. A. Subhashini, K.R. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, S.,B. Shroff, S,V. Shroff for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by FAZAL ALI, J.-This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated October 10, 1976 passed by a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court in CMA No. 14/77 whereby the appellant's writ petition filed under Article 227 of the constitution was dismissed. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer on the post of Draughtsman and he was promoted as Senior Engineer on October 1, 1976.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1913], was an employee of the respondent. The respondent was employed as a clerk in the office of the appellant. He was paid wages by the appellant to his employees at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. On reference made by the Industrial Tribunal, the respondent raised the question that the wages prescribed by the award were not payable under section 2(vi) of the Act before it was amended and substituted in the interest of social justice. The appellant contended that the provisions of section 2 (vi) were applicable to the case and that the said provision did not apply to the facts of the present case. Held, that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the amended definition of wages under section 10(1) of Act. The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant was entitled for the benefits of the said provisions. The Industrial Tribunal was also right in directing payment of wages by an industrial adjudication. The award passed by the Tribunal was not a decree of the High Court and, therefore, it could not be treated as a decree under section 15 of the Industrial Disputes Act. R. Chacko v The Labour Appellate Tribunal, Mysore, , referred to. The provisions of the [Industrial Disputes Act] were applicable only to the parties before it and not to the appellant before it. The words "the period of operation of the award" in section 2 of the Amending Act did not include the wages directed by an award. The said words clearly indicate that the legislature intended that the terms prescribed by an order, which was a decree passed by a Court, should be deemed to be a contract between the parties. The word "contract" in the context means a contract and not a contract. The expression "the terms of the contract" in Section 2(xi) meant a contract for the purpose of securing the payment of money by instalments or otherwise. The question whether the wages are payable under the award or not was a mixed question of fact and law. The Labour Court was right, therefore. The appeal is allowed and the order passed by it is set aside.

The appellant was a public servant. He was prosecuted for criminal misappropriation of the Government money and was convicted by the trial court, and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500/-. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against him by the Sessions Judge. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 409, and directed that he be tried for the offence of criminal misappropriation. The appellant filed an application before the High court for a certificate to appeal to this Court. The High court held that the prosecution was not maintainable in view of section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the provisions of section 270 of the Indian Penal Code were mandatory and, therefore, sanction under section 197 (1) was necessary. Held, that the words "in any case" occurring in section 197 of the Act were wide enough to include cases where the public servant had committed criminal misappropriation or forgery. The words "or offence" occurring therein must be construed as including a case where the accused is concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed by virtue of his office, then sanction was necessary and that would be a matter of defence on the merits, which would have to be in vestigated at the trial. The word "shall" occurring under section 270(1)(a) of Government of India Act, 1935, must be interpreted as including not only a case of criminal breach of trust but also a case for prosecution under section 420, and that therefore no sanction was required under section197(1).

The Indian Income tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) was passed by the Indian Legislature in respect of income received or accruing within British India. The assessee, a resident of an Indian State and a resident in an Indian States, filed a return of his income under section 8 of the Act on April 1, 1950, declaring that he had not earned profits or gains during the previous year relevant to the assessment year ending March 31, 1951, and that he was liable to tax under section 10. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee as an Indian citizen and also as an individual. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the income received by the appellant from the business in which he had been carrying on was not taxable in British India and that the profits and gains arising under section 3 or section 4 must be deemed to have accrued or arisen within British Indian. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an industrial undertaking of the respondent. The appellant was an employee of the Bombay region and was working as a Head Office in the Bombay area. On November 1, 1957, the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, issued a notification under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') fixing the age of retirement at 60. The respondent challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay. The High Court held that the appellant was not justified in fixing the date of superannuation at 60 and that it was not open to the Tribunal to go into the question whether the respondent had been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. On appeal, this Court reversed the decision of the High court and held that there was no justification for the Tribunal in holding that the respondent was justified in making the impugned order. The present appeal is directed against the said judgment of the Calcutta High Court. Before dealing with the question as to whether the appellant should be given an effective opportunity to explain the circumstances appearing in the evidence on record, we may refer to the relevant provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. Section 10(2) of that Act provides: "10. (1) The Central Government or any State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. (2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:- (a) the age and retirement of an employee; (b) the conditions of service of employees other than those referred to in sub-section (1); (c) the procedure to be followed by the Tribunal under section 11; (d) the powers of the Tribunal for the purpose of hearing appeals against orders passed by it under this Act; (e) the power to make rules under clause (b), clause (c), clause(d) and clause (e). (f) the manner in which the appeal shall be heard and disposed of.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi for offences under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and section 412 of the [Indian Penal Code]. The prosecution case was that on December 8, 1967, the appellants were found in possession of a large number of goods of the same type. On the basis of the information given by the accused, the police arrested them and sent them to the Police Station. The police seized the articles from the appellants. The appellants were charged with having committed offences under sections 395 and 412 of Indian Penal code. The prosecution examined four witnesses. The defence was that the goods in question were stolen from some other source and the goods were being taken away by the cartmen. The trial court held that the accused had not been found guilty of the offence under section 412, Indian Penal. On appeal the High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the appellants under sections 396 and 412, I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court also confirmed the conviction and sentence passed on the appellants by the trial court. In this appeal it is contended that the prosecution case is not established beyond reasonable doubt and therefore the accused are entitled to benefit of doubt. It was further submitted that the evidence of the witnesses clearly shows that the appellants had been found in conscious possession of the goods which were stolen. The learned counsel for the State, however, supported the judgment of the High court. The evidence on record shows that from each one of the persons who were the dacoits, the articles were found and the accused were found to be in possession thereof. It is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the appellants are guilty of committing offences under Section 396 or 412, IPC. The only point urged before us by Mr. S. N. Mukherjee, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants was that there was no evidence to show that the articles in question had been stolen from any other source. It may be pointed out that the High Courts have taken a contrary view and held that it is not possible to say that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. The fact that the appellant was found in exclusive possession of some of the articles, does not mean that he was guilty of an offence under Section 412, Penal Code. The question whether there was a dacoity or not has been considered by this Court in several cases and it is difficult to see how the evidence on the record shows any such evidence. In the present case, we are satisfied that the circumstances show that there were no other circumstances which would justify the conviction of the accused under section 396, IPC and section 411, I..P. C., and they have been rightly convicted by the High. Court.

The petitioner was a dealer in poisons. He purchased the poisons from the Government of India and sold it to the petitioner for sale by him. The petitioner purchased the said poisons on payment of Rs. 1,000/- as price of the poadia. The said amount was paid by the petitioner to the Government. On the basis of the said amount, a complaint was filed against the petitioner under Section 7 of the Act and the proceedings were taken in respect of the same. The High Court held that the petitioner had no right to carry on the business of sale and sale of poisons and that he was not entitled to sell the poples of poadia as poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle. It further held that there was no evidence to show that the said poison was a poison for purposes of the levy of tax under the Act. The Court, therefore, quashed the proceedings and directed the petitioner's release on bail. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the trial court and dismissed the petition filed by the appellant. In this Court, it was contended that the provisions of the [Indian Medical Council Act, 1956] were not applicable to the case as the said Act had been repealed by the Indian Medical Council (Amendment) Act, 1951. HELD: The High Courts have jurisdiction to regulate the import and export of poples in any local area in which the use of such poison for purpose of sale or sale is to be regulated. [775 H] In the instant case, the petitioner purchased a poisons under the provisions contained in Section 2(x) of the Indian Medicine Act, 1939. The question whether the said provision was applicable to him was not considered by the High Courts and the Court held it to be a 'poppy substance' for purposes other than those specified in clause (x) thereof. [750 H] The provisions of Sections 3 and 4 of the Central Act were not attracted to the facts of the case. Section 2 (x), as amended, was applicable only to the cases where the possession or sale of any poison is prohibited by law. [751 G] In view of the fact that the Act had not been repealed, it could not be said that the provision in question was a 'packaged medicine for the purposes of Section 2 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

The assessee, a firm of which the Bombay firm was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. K.K. & Co., was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") for the assessment year 1954-55. The assessee claimed that the amounts received by him from the Bombay firms were not loans made in the ordinary course of the business of the firm and therefore he was entitled to a deduction of Rs. 2,68,385/ under section 10(2) (xi) of the Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount was not sent to the Bombay Firm as loan made in his ordinary course. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended by the assessee that the sums received by the Bombay partnership were not agricultural loans but were advanced in the normal course of business of a firm which was carrying out the normal business of money lending. The Tribunal held that the sum of Rs 2, 68,385/- was not a loan made by the firm to the said Bombay firm and it was not an agricultural loan. On further appeal, it upheld the order passed by the Income Tax Officer. In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held: "In view of this finding, we are of the opinion that the assessee is entitled to deduction of the amount received by it from the said firm as loans made for the purpose of the partnership business. The question referred to us is answered accordingly." The High Court, in further appeal filed by the Revenue, has taken a different view and held that on the facts of the case, the amounts were not sent by the appellant to the Hyderabad firm as loan was made in its ordinary course and therefore they were not chargeable to income-tax under section 11(2)(xi) read with section 10 (2). The High court also took the same view. In this Court, on behalf of the Revenue it was submitted that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the said amounts were agricultural loans and not loans given by the said two firms. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The amount received from the Hyderabad Firm was not agricultural loan but was advanced in cash to the assessee. [557F] 1.2 In the instant case, there is no evidence on record that the appellant had taken any loan for the purposes of the said business. There is also no evidence that the money sent by it was utilised in the course of its business. [506 G] 1:3 The Tribunal has rightly held that it was a loan given to the appellant by the Hyderabad firms and therefore it was entitled under section 5(2). [528 D] 2.1 In the present case, as the amount of Rs 3,68-385/was not sent in the regular course of moneylending business, the assessee was entitled for deduction of that amount from his income. The High Courts have rightly held against the appellant. [504 G] 2:2 It is well settled that a loan is given by a person who has taken it in the usual course of his business and he cannot be said to have taken it on behalf or for the benefit of the assessee, unless there is evidence to show that the loan was advanced to him as loan. The appellant, a hotel, was granted a lease of five acres of land in the village of the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The appellant applied to the Government for grant of four acres of lands in the said area. The Government rejected the application on the ground that it was not reasonable and in public interest to do so. On appeal, the Division Bench held that the land was not required by the State for the purpose of establishing a Five star hotel and that the decision taken was not unreasonable or arbitrary. It further held that there was no material before the Government to show that the construction was made in the interest of public interest. The Division Bench also held that it is not possible to say that the Government was bound to advertise the land for the purposes of establishing an industry within the State and invite those interested to come up with the said proposal. In this view, the High Court set aside the order passed by the learned Single Judge and directed the Government of West Bengal to grant four acres in favour of the appellant. The matter was carried in appeal to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The decision taken by the Government is not unreasonable nor arbitrary. [675 H] 1.2 The decision of the Division bench is not arbitrary or unreasonable and that it does not call for any interference. [775 B] 1:3. The question whether the land in question was required by public interest or not, has to be decided on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant considerations have been taken into account by the Court while deciding the matter. [750 D] 1.:4. In the instant case, the appellant had applied for four acres and five acres in the open market. The State Government was not bound to advertised the land. It is only a policy decision which can be considered as reasonable and fair. [751 H] 2:1. The High Court was right in holding that there is no material on record to show whether the construction is made in public or otherwise. [753 D] 2.2 In the present case, it is clear that the appellant has made out a case for an injunction restraining the Government from selling the land and the appellant is not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. [764 G] 2.:2. The decision in the case of [The State of West BENGAL vs. the Taj Mahal Hotel] , referred to by the Division Benches, was not a good law. In that case, this Court held that if the land is required for the public purpose, it would be open to the State to sell the land to the public and invite them to come with the highest price. [754 G] 3:3 The decision was not arbitrary but was based on an unreasonable or irrational consideration of public interests. The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee had a son and a daughter. The father of the assessee died in the year of account, i.e., on April 1, 1955. The mother of the deceased, who was the wife of the husband of the appellant, died in December, 1956. The income from the said property was assessed as income tax. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer and dismissed the appeal. In an appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that section 10 of the Act did not apply to the gifts made by the deceased to his son and that the High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The gift made by a Hindu Undivided family is valid and the sum of Rs.1 lakh paid by the father to his wife, K, by way of trust or otherwise, is available to the firm. [675 H] 2. Section 10 of Act does not apply in the case of gifts made on behalf the assessee. The object of section 10 is to prevent a person from being credited with any amount which may be available to that firm for the purpose of his business and that is why section 10 was enacted. [775 B] 3. In order to attract section 10, it must be shown that the assessee has a family or a company which is not a banking company or which has no overdraft facility, by mere book entries in the account books of the Hindu undivided families with Rs.50,000 and credited the same in the personal account of his son. [750 C] 4. The High Court erred in answering question in favour of the respondent. [751 D] 5. Section 11 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961 does not come into play in the present case because it is not attracted to the facts of the present appeal. [753 H] 6. The provisions of section 11 are applicable only to the income tax proceedings and not to any other proceedings. [754 G] 7. The question whether section 10 applies to gifts made in favour or by way o which may have no overdraft facilities, by merely book entries is a matter for the Income tax authorities to decide. [752 H] 8. Section 12 of the 1922 Act does apply to gifts of Rs 50,000 to his daughter and to her wife respectively. The fact that the father of an assessee has not a bank or a financial institution or a banking corporation or any other body corporate which has a overdraft facility is a relevant factor in deciding whether section 11 applies to the gift made on his behalf. [764 H] 9. Section 13 of the 1961 Act does no more than refer to the effect that section 11 is applicable to gifts, and not otherwise. [758 G] 10. The language of section 12 is clear and unambiguous. It does not require any further elaboration. [759 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1987. The appellant was a member of the Bihar Judicial Service. He was appointed as District Judge in the State of Bihar and was posted at Patna. On October 10, 1966 he was promoted to the post of District Judges. The High Court held that Shri B.K. Patro, the then Chief Justice of the High Court, was not entitled to hold the post as a law secretary, deputy law Secretary or superintendent and legal remembrancer and that the transfer of District Judge from Patna to Patna was illegal. On November 10, 1967 he was transferred to Patna. The State Government issued an order on October 10 1966 transferring Shri B K Patro from Patna. He filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the said order. The learned single judge held that the order of transfer was not valid and quashed the order. On appeal by the State, the Division Bench reversed the judgment of the learned single Judge and dismissed the writ petition. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were not competent to issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ directing the Government to transfer a district judge from Patna and to hold that the said transfer was illegal and void. HELD: (i) The order of the Governor dated October 10 1967 transferring Shri P.C. Pathe, the Chief Justice, was valid. [775 H] (ii) The High Courts are not competent under article 235 to issue any writ of certiorari or other appropriate writs directing the State Government to make appointments, promotion and posting to the cadre of district judges but in posting Shri BK Patro who is posted to the district courts, it is for the High courts to decide whether the said appointment was valid or not. [750 H] The High court was competent under Article 235 to direct that the District Judges should be transferred from Patna as well as Patna to the State cadre. [751 A] (iii) The transfer of a district Judge from one district to another is illegal and invalid. [751 D] (iv) The power of the Chief justice, in terms of article 235, is vested in the Governor. The power to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Constitution is vested with the High Power.
