The trial court held that the sale was not valid but it directed the pre emption to be given to the co sharers as well as to the tenants. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal before this Court, the appellants contended that the High court erred in holding that the sales were invalid because they had not been sold jointly by all the co co sharer and the tenants were entitled to pre emurn the property. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sale was valid and it was not open to the two judge Bench to hold that the transaction was not invalid because of the provisions of section 15(1)(b) of the Act. [775 H] 2. Section 15(l)(a) of The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 provides that where a partition is made between co shares and their respective shares are specified in clause 'fourthly' of section15(1), then the right of pre emptee to pre- emption shall be deemed to have been vested in the sons or daughters of the vendors. [750 H] 3. The expression 'other co shars' in section 15 (1)(a), is not defined in the Act and it has no meaning in law. It means a co sharienner who is a co co- sharer. [751 A] 4. Section 16(1) of Hindu Succession, Act, which provides that if any person dies after all the shares are acquired jointly by one or more co co co mpany, he shall be entitled to partition in accordance with the provisions contained in section 14 of the Indian Succession Act. The words 'other' and 'thirdly' have been used in section 16(l) (b). [751 B] 5. Section 17(1A) of Act provides that when a partition has been made between all the joint land co mpsenants, the right to pre co mptee shall be extinguished if the other co co sfsion is not by all or any of them jointly. [75 H; 76 B] 6. The word 'other', in section 17(lA) means a person who is not a co mpohidar and includes a co-sharer. [76 D] 7. Section 18(1B) of Indian Successions Act, 1925 provides that the right conferred by this section shall be subject to the provisions therein contained in the said Act. It does not apply to any other co mmplainant. [77 E] 8. The question whether a partition can be made between the co mpppants and their joint land is a mixed question of law and fact. [78 G] 9. Section 14(1-A) provides that in case of partition, the share of each co co tfpntee shall not be divided by metes and bounds. [79 H; 80 A] 10. The provisions contained therein are applicable to a partition made between a co tpnts and their separate shares. [80 G] 11. The provision is not attracted if the sons and daughters of each of them are not co mfsideres. [81 H; 82 A] 12. The appellants filed a suit for partition of the property in which they claimed that they were entitled to 1/3rd share each in the property and that the sale deeds executed by them in favour of the alienees were valid and binding on the alienee. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the alienations made by the alienors were valid, but the alienor was not entitled to any interest in the properties. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the alienation was valid and the alienes had become owners of the properties by virtue of the sale deed executed by the appellants. The High Court further held that as the alienations were valid they were binding on Seshiah and in view of the fact that there was a compromise between the parties, the suit should be disposed of and the terms of the compromise should form part of the order to settle all the equities between the appellants and the purchasers. In appeal by special leave, the Court HELD: 1. The sale deeds were valid. [775 H] 2.1 The High court was in error in holding that as there was no compromise between parties the suit must be disposed at the earliest. [750 A] 2(i) The High Courts and the courts below have not properly appreciated the fact of the case and the trial court has rightly held that since there was an allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which we have found to be valid, the sale was valid. The appellants were entitled only to get possession of the entire property in suit including those which were covered by the sale. [751 B] 2.(ii) The alienations were invalid and the alienations are valid. It is not open to the alieners to contend that they had become owner of the lands by virtue or under the sale, but should be satisfied by the purchasers before the Sub Registrar on the basis of the record made by him. [751 D] 2 (iii) The alienation was invalid and no question of payment or adjustment of mesne profits arose. [764 G] 3.1 In the instant case there is a compromise in favour between the appellant and Seshiahay, the aliener. The transaction was valid as it was not registered by the Sub- Registrar on behalf of Seshihah. [754 A] 3.(i) There was no allegation of any payment of money to Sudarshan Kumar Gupta which he had become entitled to withdraw the amounts from the properties in suit and that there is no evidence to show that the aliene had become the owner of those properties. [752 B] (ii) In view of this finding, the appellants were not entitled for any interest on the amount of Rs 1 lakh. [758 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1989. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was engaged in the manufacture of glass and glass products. The company was registered as a limited company with the Registrar of Companies, Bombay. On April 1, 1976, the Company issued a notice to the workmen of the Company for payment of retrenchment compensation under section 25F of the Act. The workmen raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to get the benefit of sick leave under section 24(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and accordingly granted relief to the appellant in respect of the period from January 1, 1975 to March 31, 1976. On appeal by the company, the High Court of Gujarat confirmed the order of the Tribunal. The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the correctness of the decision of the High court. This Court held that section 24 (1) was not applicable to the case of the workmen and that the benefit under the Act could be granted only in the case where the benefits were granted for an industrial purpose. In view of the finding recorded by the Tribunal that the appellant was entitled to relief for sick leave, the question whether the workmen should be given the benefit for a period of two days in the garb of sick Leave was not decided. The High Court held: "The Industrial Disputes Tribunal has rightly held that a workman who is entitled to sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance can be granted for a further period of one day, if he is found to have been sickness during the period of his employment. In this view of matter, the order passed by the Industrial Tribunal is not sustainable." The appellant challenged the correctness or otherwise of the said decision of this Court before this court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 24(2) of Act does not apply to the cases of sick industrial establishments. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunals have given a finding that the sickness benefit was granted for the first two days of sickness under the second proviso to section 49 of the act. The question whether an industrial establishment should be entitled to claim relief for the period prior to the date of its commencement or not is a matter which has to be decided by the Labour Court and it cannot be said that the Industrial disputes Tribunal has given a decision on the issue of sickness benefit. [750 H] 2.1 In the case before us, the appellant had raised an Industrial dispute which had been referred to a Tribunal for its adjudication. It was not necessary, in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit to the workman under the provisions of the [Industrial Disputes Act]. The question as to whether the industrial dispute was pending on the date when the Act came into force or not was not considered by this Court in the said case. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 4.8.1989 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 1125 of 1986. V.M. Tarkunde, S.K. Mehta, R.S. Pathak, P.H. Parekh, Ms. A. Subhashini, M.R. Shroff for the Appellant. K.T. Shah, S K Patel and G.L. Sanghi for the Respondent. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated April 4, 1989 of the Bombay High Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant challenging the validity of the order dated April 5, 1989 passed by this court in Special civil Application No 1125/86. The respondent had raised a dispute which related to the period between January 1. 1975 to May 31, 1975.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. The order of detention was made on June 30, 1971. The grounds were served on the appellant on December 7, 1971 and he was arrested on January 8, 1972. On February 9, 1972, the appellant filed a petition under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the order of his detention. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the grounds furnished to the appellant in paragraph 12 of the affidavit were not sufficient to enable him to make an effective representation and to communicate the decision to the detenu. It was further held that the ground contained in the affidavit did not constitute a material change in the circumstances which had been disclosed by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the order was passed without giving him an opportunity of making a representation and that the failure to furnish the grounds did not vitiate the detention. It is contended that the decision of the detaining authority was vitiated because it was not in public interest to disclose facts which were considered against the appellant. The learned counsel for the respondents, however, supported the order passed by the High court on the first ground. In the first place, it was urged that the appellant had been detained under the provisions of section 3 (1) (a) of Conservation of foreign Exchange and Act, 1973 and therefore he could not be said to have been furnished with a copy of the grounds of detention. Secondly, it is contended by the learned counsel that the High Curt has erred in law in holding that article 22(6) of Constitution of India was violated inasmuch as the appellant did not make a representation against the order before the Advisory Board and therefore the order should be quashed. The second contention urged on behalf of the respondents is that the power to detain under section3 (1)(a) cannot be exercised by the detaining authorities in public interests. It has been held by this Court in [Shanker Chandra Bose vs State of West Bengal] , that the right to make a proper representation guaranteed under article 22 (5) of our Constitution is not affected by the provisions contained in section 3 of the Act for the reasons given therein. The third contention urged by the respondents was rejected by this court holding that it was open to the detaining Authority to consider the grounds on which the detention order was made and to convey the decision, if any, to the petitioner. In our opinion, the second contention also cannot be accepted as well. The question whether the appellant should be directed to furnish a copy or not is a matter of policy and in the absence of such policy, it would be open to an aggrieved person to make representation against his detention and to produce evidence in support thereof. It may be that the detaining Authorities may consider the facts and circumstances of the case before them and if they are satisfied that the detention is necessary, they should communicate the grounds to the person detained, but that does not mean that the authority concerned has to furnish him the information which he has given in the form in which it was required by law. The right to be furnished with the particulars of the facts considered against him cannot be said that the said information is vague or indefinite and therefore it would amount to denial of all the particulars and therefore, the order under section 5 of the COFEPOSA should be set aside.

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army. He was appointed as a member in the Indian Air Force on January 1, 1954. On March 31, 1955, he was promoted to the Indian Civil Service and was posted at the Indian Police Service. On April 30, 1956, he served under the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, Department of Home and Civil Supplies, New Delhi. He retired from service on May 28, 1957. On June 1, 1958, he filed a petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Madras Bench, praying for a direction to the Union of India to make rules for the removal of an officer from the Indian civil Service. The Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, were ultra vires the . Constitution and the rules framed thereunder. On appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court held that the words "subject to the provisions" occurring in section 19(1) (a) of the Act were wide enough to include within its ambit the words 'subject to' and 'the rules' used in s. 19(2). The appellant filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Tribunal. This Court held, that the expression "subject" occurring therein was wide enough and it did not mean that there should be rules, and that the rule framed thereunder must be ultra vires. It was further held that in view of the provisions contained in s.. 19(3) of Act 14 of 1955, the Central Government could remove an officer without being tried and convicted by court martial if he was a junior commissioned officer or warrant officer. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The words " subject to the provision" occurringin section 19 (1)(a) are wide enough not to include in its ambit within its scope the words used in section 20 of the General Clauses Act. [675 H] 2. The expression 'subject' occurring in s 19(4) is wide enough, and it means that there must be rules and regulations for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions mentioned therein. [775 B] 3. The word "subject", as used in the Act, must mean that the Central Govt. has no power to remove an Officer from the service. It does not mean merely that the rules made thereunder must also be ultravires. [750 H] 4. The language of s. 20(1)(b) is clear and unambiguous. The use of the words in the context indicates that there can be a valid rule or regulation for the purposes of carrying out the provisions specified therein. The Central Govt., has no authority to remove a person from the Service. [751 H] 5. The power to make regulations under s. 16 is not subject to any other provision of the Constitution. [751 D] 6. The term "subjects" occurring ins. 19 (4) does not include within it, but it means only that there shall be rules or regulations for such removal. [752 H] 7. The provisions contained therein are wide and do not mean anything more than what is in the nature of a rule or regulations. [754 A] 8. The question whether the words, "subject matter" occurring under s 19 (3) are limited to the matters mentioned in sub-section (1) of section 20 does not arise for consideration in this case. [764 G] 9. The provision contained in section 16 is wide and it includes within its purview, the words subject to' which are in the statute must be read as 'subject'. [756 H] 10. The intention of the legislature was clear that the word " subject" occurring at the time of s.. 20(2) should be construed as referring to the words of the section. [758 G] 11.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was assessed to octroi duty by the Deputy Commissioner of the District. The appellant filed an appeal against the assessment before the Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, New Delhi. The Secretary to Government of Punjab, Departmentof Revenue, issued a notice dated January 14, 1964 under s. 8(1) of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948, requiring the appellant to show cause why the tax levied by it should not be recovered from him. The respondent filed an objection to the said notice on the ground that the levy was illegal and that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, who heard the objections, held that the tax was not leviable by reason of the fact that the tea imported into octroi limits was crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. On appeal the Secretary of State for India, who allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Assistant Commissioner and directed the appellant's refund of the tax collected from him with interest at the rate of 6% per annum. The case was then taken up by the Government in appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that s. 5(b) of Punjab General sales Tax Act had no application to the facts of the case and accordingly dismissed the appeal. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the provisions contained in s. 3(b), (1) and (2) of that Act were mandatory in character and did not apply to the case. The learned counsel for the respondent, however, supported the view taken by the High. Court. Section 5(a) of this Act provides that the Government may, after considering the objections received under sub-s.(1), make an order directing that the octroi duty or fee leviable on such tea shall be levied from the date specified in the notice issued under s 8(2). The learned Counsel for the appellant contended that the word "shall" used in s 5(c) of Act No. 1 of 1948, meant that the Collector had to make an enquiry into the matter and he was not bound by the provisions thereof. It is true that the words "may be deemed to have been substituted for " must mean " must be read as " must have been inserted in the statute itself. But the question whether the word 'shall' used in the section should be construed as mandatory or directory does not arise at all. The word "may" used therein is not defined in the Act. It has to be interpreted according to its ordinary meaning and it cannot be read in a manner which would lead to an absurd result.

The appellant, a company, was an employee of the respondent. The respondent was employed as a conductor in the appellant's factory at Dhanbad. He was dismissed from service on January 17, 1957. On March 18, 1958, he filed a petition under section 33 of the Act before the Labour Court, Delhi, for permission to dismiss him from service. The Labour Court held that the notice dated December 6, 1959, terminating his services was illegal and directed reinstatement of the appellant with effect from January 17. The appellant challenged the order of the Labour court by filing an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal and remanded the case to the Labour Commissioner for fresh disposal in accordance with law. On remand, the Labour Officer passed a fresh order on March 18. 1958. The appellants filed a writ petition in this court challenging the order dated March 18,. 1958. This Court held in that case that section 12(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act was not applicable to the appellant and the termination of his services by the respondent was illegal. It was further held that as the notice terminating his service was illegal, the provisions of section 12 (6) were not attracted. The appeal filed by the appellants was dismissed by this Court. In the present case, the dispute between the parties was whether the notice was valid or not and if so, whether the termination was legal or not. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether section 12 contemplates a fresh notice to terminate the services of the workmen concerned. Section 12(5) of Act provides that where an industrial dispute has been referred to the appropriate Government under section 10, it shall be deemed to have terminated the service of the workman concerned immediately before the date on which the report was made by the Conciliation Officer and the provisions in this behalf are applicable to him. The contention raised by the appellant is that section 11(6)(b) provides for a fresh enquiry and if proceedings were not closed, it would be open to the respondent to contend that the termination is illegal. Section 11(5), as it stood at the time when the notice of termination was issued, reads: "11(5). If an industrial workman is dismissed or removed from service, he shall be liable to pay compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months." The contention of the appellants is that under section 12, the notice must be given by the appropriate government and if it is not given by a party, the termination would be illegal. If the notice is valid, the provision of section 11 (5) will have no application to the case. Section 13(6), as amended, provides for an enquiry into the conduct of an employee in respect of any misconduct or violation of the provisions contained in the Act. The proviso to that section provides that if the employer fails to give notice under section 11 within the period specified therein, it will be open for the respondent, to contend before the labour court that the order terminating his employment was illegal or invalid. Section 14(6A) provides that no workman shall be dismissed from the service without giving him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him and if he is not found guilty of any such misconduct, he can be punished with imprisonment for a period which may extend to three months or with fine. The effect of section 14(5)(b), as substituted by Act No. 16 of 1958, is that where the employer has failed to give the notice under [section 11], it will not be open either to the employer or the workman to contend in the matter before the court that termination of the services was legal and valid. The provision of Section 12 (5A) does not contemplate a fresh proceeding for the same purpose.

The petitioner was arrested on the basis of a criminal charge and was released on bail. The order of detention was passed against him on the ground that he was in jail for more than three months. He was also found to be in jail. On his conviction, he was released by the competent authority. The State Government issued an order of preventive detention on the same day i.e. on 25th December, 1985. The petitioner challenged the said order before this Court and prayed that the order of the State Government be quashed. This Court held that the grounds of detention were vague and indefinite and there was no material to indicate that the detaining authority was satisfied with the facts and circumstances of the case. In the instant case, the detenu was in custody for more or less three months and he was likely to be released on his executing a bond for Rs. 50,000/- with two sureties, one of whom was in detention as well as another in jail and the other in jail, if released. The Court held: "The grounds of the order are vague and uncertain and do not indicate that it is passed on the satisfaction of the detaining or the detaining authorities. In this case, therefore, the detention order was bad and on relevant considerations, the petitioner could not have been put into preventive custody." The Court further observed that in the facts of this case the grounds were vague as well. It was held that there was nothing to indicate the fact that the detenu had already been released by a competent authority and he had also surrendered before the detention. In these circumstances, it was held: "...The detaining authority has not given any explanation as to why the petitioner was in judicial custody for three months." The court further observed: "In the instant cases, there is no statement that the detention of the detenu under the Act was on proper consideration and he could be released or that the possibility of his release was taken into consideration by the detaining and the detaining Authority in accordance with law. In our opinion, therefore the order passed by the State government on the very day i..e. 25th January, 1985 is bad and illegal and it is liable to be quashed." The petitioner filed an appeal against the said decision of this Court before the Supreme Court which was dismissed. Hence this petition.

The appellant, a dealer in gold ornaments and articles of gold, was carrying on business as a money lender. He was prosecuted for the offence under sec. 28 of the Act. The prosecution was launched against him for the contravention of the provisions of the Gold Control Act. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed against the appellant. The appellant filed an application before the High court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that the power conferred upon the Administrator under secs. 5(1) of the said Act was not exercised in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act and that the Administrator had no authority to grant or renew a license to a dealer. The High Court held that the appellant could not be heard to contend that he was entitled to the protection of the relevant provisions of law under the Act as he was not a moneylender. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the provisions in the Gold (Control) Act were not applicable to him and that, therefore, the Administrator was competent to grant the license to the dealer. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Administrator by sec. 5 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act is a power which is not an absolute one. [557F] 2.1 The power under sec.. 5(2) of that Act is not a power to grant a license but it is a discretionary power vested in the Administrator and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [506G] 2:2 Section 28 of Act provides for an appeal against any order passed by the Administrator, if the order is passed by him under secti ons. 29(1), 30(3) and 31(4). The power to make a rule under sec.(5) is not absolute but is subject to the condition that the rules made by the Government in exercise of its powers under secl. 5 (2) are strictly speaking applicable to the case. [657F D] 2 2:3 Section 28 does not confer any arbitrary or uncanalised power on the administrator. The Administrator has no authority either to grant, renew a licence or to renew a lease. He is bound by the policy and purpose of the statute under which he is empowered to grant license.

The appellant, who was the manager of a religious endowment, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court held that the properties were purchased by the appellant from his father and that he had been removed from office by other persons who were in management of the temple. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the fact that the alienee was a minor at the time of his death was not conclusive as to whether he was a Hindu or an individual. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in reversing the decision and holding that the question as to who should be deemed to be the previous manager of the trust did not arise for consideration. [557 F] (2) The fact that a suit was brought by the present appellant against his father or the family was a mixed question of fact and law, and so, it could not be said that more than 12 years have elapsed since the date of the removal of the previous Manager who transferred the properties in question. [506 G] (3) The question as regards the applicability of section 52 of the Act to a case where an alienee is dead or cannot be deemed by any other person who was not in management for the past 27 years, and the High court was in wrong in reversing that decision. [657 H] (4) Section 52 of The Act does not apply to cases where the alienor has been removed, but it applies to cases of removal from office. [757 D] (5) The position is well settled that a person who is dead and cannot be considered as being a Hindu by any one who was in management or control of the property must be deemed for all purposes to have been duly appointed trustees. [613 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated April 20, 1966 of the Bombay High Court in First Appeal No.. 1123 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma, for the appellant. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General of India, K. J. John, P. H. Parekh and R. Hathi, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a Hindu Religious Endowment. He filed an application under section 52(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') before the High Curt of Bombay challenging the validity of the order passed by respondent No 1 on the ground that the said order was without jurisdiction and also that the order was not a nullity. The High C Court held that section 52 did not apply in the case where the alienation was made by the manager who transferred his properties to other persons, and that the appellant was entitled to claim partition of all the properties and that therefore he was entitled for partition. In appeal to this Court it was argued on behalf (1)[1964] 6 S.C.R. 836 that section 51(2) of The Madras Hindu Endowment Act, 1932 (hereinafter called 'the said Act') did not come into force in the State of Bombay and that as the appellant had been appointed trustees by respondent no 1 he could not claim partition under section 53 of the said Act. Dismissing this appeal, Held: (i) Section 51(1)(a) of Madras Hindu Endowments Act 1932 does not affect the rights of the manager to be a trustee in respect of the management of any property which is vested in him and that such a person has been appointed by respondent 1 as trustees by the said section.

The appellant, a firm of which the respondent was a partner, filed an application under Section 6 of the Act for a declaration that the licence in respect of Apsara Theatre was granted to Shri Ved Gupta and that it had become necessary for him to operate the Cinema. The District Magistrate by his order dated December 29, 1977 directed the suspension of cinema licence in favour of the firm Apsar Theatre. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order passed by the District Magistrate on the ground that the said order was violative of the principles of natural justice. It held that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order dated January 29, 1980. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was not vitiated by any error of law. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The power to suspend a licence under Section 5 of the Apsarsara Theatre Act is conferred only by Section 6 F of the said Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said Section are present, the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction to make an order suspending the licence. [505 G] 1.2 The High Courts have held that under the provisions of the Constitution the power to make orders for the suspension or cancellation of a licence is conferred by Section 5 F of Act No. 16 of 1976 and the Rules framed thereunder The impugned order was passed in exercise of the powers conferred on the District Police Officer under Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses Act, 1957. [506 G] 2.1 It is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the said power could be exercised by the licensing authorities or the licensing officer in a case where an order was made by the Superintendent of Police under Section 4 of the Control Order. The only other ground stated by the High Courts for quashing the order of suspension of the licence was that the licensee had been convicted and sentenced to undergo a sentence of imprisonment for a period of one year and six months respectively. [504 G] 3.2 It is well settled that in an appeal against an order passed under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, the power conferred on a Court of Law under Section 8 of the Central Act is not available to the High court. The said power can be exercised only by the State Government or the District Officer and not by any other authority. [405 G B] 3:3 It is also well settled law that in a matter where an authority has no power to pass an order, it has no jurisdiction under Section 9 of the General Clauses act as one of the grounds for quashing an order made by a Court. The power conferred upon the District and the State Police Officer to make the order is not a power which can be said to have been exercised by any person other than the licensee. [498 G] 4. In the instant case, the licence has been suspended in exercise or discharge of the duties imposed on it under Section 12 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The question whether there was an order of suspending the licensee is a matter for the State to decide and not the issue whether the licence is valid or not. [500 G] 5. In view of the provisions contained in Section 6F of the Indian General Clauses, it is not possible to hold that the power under Section 11 of the Public Premises (Eviction) Act is available to a licensee. The order passed on December 29/30, 1977 was not challenged by the appellant before the High C Court and the writ petitions were dismissed. [605 G-H] 6. The appellants, the appellants, and the respondents, were tenants of the mills in respect of the lands in question. The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that they had become the owners of the said lands by virtue of an agreement to sell dated 13th February, 1955, executed between them and the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled to terminate the lease under section 12 of the Act and that the respondent was not liable to pay any compensation for the period of the lease. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of section 12 were applicable to the case and that it was open to the Custodian to cancel the lease in favour of the appellants. The High Court further held that under section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract is not void if it is not made by the owner or the agent of the owner, but is made by a person who has no authority under the law to do so. On this finding, the appeal was allowed and the suit filed by the appellants was dismissed. The present appeal is directed against that decision. The question for determination in this appeal is whether the provisions contained in section 12 are applicable to cases where the lease is not executed by the evacuee or the Custodian, as the case may be. Section 12 provides that no person shall be entitled to cancel a lease of any property if he has made a lease by himself or his agent and that power under section 13 is not exercised by him in good faith. The respondent contended that the suit was not maintainable because the appellants had become owners of lands in respect thereof, and that therefore the provisions were applicable only to cases of leases executed by them. Held: (i) Section 12 does not apply to cases which are not covered by section 12. It is clear from the language of section 13 that it applies to cases in which the lease was not executed either by the Custodian or by a third party and that such a case must be decided on the terms of the section as it stood prior to the amendment. The provisions contained therein apply only to situations where the property is not transferred by the evacuees, and no other law for the time being in force. (ii) Section 13 does not affect the rights of the parties in so far as they relate to the purchase by them of the mill and the factory is one of the matters specified in section 10. The words "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law" are clear enough to cover cases where a lease is executed by a Custodian or an officer appointed under the Act to sell the mills and the factories. (iii) Section 14 does not bar the jurisdiction of the High Courts to entertain such suits.

The appellant was a member of the Board of Revenue. He filed an application under Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act, 1956 for setting aside the order of the Sub Divisional Officer dated 5th May, 1976 and the Board dismissed the said application on the ground that the land in question was not agricultural land. The High Court held that the provisions of the Act of 1955 were applicable to the appellant and the order passed by the Board was illegal. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated 5 th May, 1975. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the Land-Revenue Act had no application to the facts of the case. The Division Bench held that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the said Act and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh constituted one unit and not two units and, therefore, the Board's order dated 14th April, 1975 was illegal and void. The State filed an appeal against the judgment of the learned Single judge before the Division Bench of the High court which was dismissed by the impugned judgment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 Section 9 is a general provision in respect of the executive control and superintendence over all revenue courts. It does not apply to the executive power of the State. [775 H] 1.2 The provisions of Section 224 of the Government of India Act, 1915 are applicable to all revenue Courts except the judicial authorities. The Board of the Revenue was competent to determine the ceiling area for the appellant in law. [750 A] 1:3. Under Section 9, the State Government has general power of superintendence and control over all Revenue courts including the District Court. The provisions contained in Chapter II B of Part III of the Constitution are applicable only to the judicial officers. [751 D] 1 Whether a particular provision is mandatory or directory depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If it is not mandatory, then the Board has general powers of superintendence over the entire revenue courts including District Court and the High Courts have general power to make rules for regulating the procedure of such courts. [751 H] 2.1 The provisions in Chapter I B of Volume III of Government of INDIA Act, 1919 are applicable in respect to all Revenue Courts except those which are specifically excluded by Section 224. The applicant Raghubir singh and his sons were constituted one and not three units and not five units. The application was filed under Section 10 of the land revenue Act. [761 H; 76 A] 2:2. Under the provisions contained therein, the provisions in the Land revenue Act have no application.

The appellant, a newspaper establishment, was incorporated in the year 1947. The respondent, a Pressman employed by the appellant, was appointed as a clerk in the office of the Chief Commissioner of Sales Tax, Orissa, on January 1, 1948. He was paid a salary of Rs. 10,000 per month. On March 31, 1949, he was served with a notice under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and he was asked to show cause why his services should not be terminated by an order dated May 2, 1950. The appellant replied to the said show cause notice on April 5, 1950, denying the allegations made against him in the said notice. On June 30, 1950 the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Orissa challenging the validity of the said order and praying for quashing the said proceedings. The High Court dismissed the writ petition by its judgment dated July 14, 1951. On further appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings on the ground that the appellant had not complied with the provisions of section 7 of the Act. HELD: (i) Section 7(2)(a) of The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1950 provides for a declaration that the said Act is void and non est in so far as it affects the rights of the employees to be paid sales tax by the State Legislature under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [775 H] (ii) Section 8(2) of Act No. 1 of 1950 provides that the provisions contained in the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any law other than this Act. The said section reads: "8. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an employer has been served with an order under clause (a) or clause (b) of subsection (3) of section 8, the provisions thereof shall have no effect." [776 H] In the instant case, the appellant was served a notice on May 2. 1950, and he filed a petition for quashing of the proceedings. On July 30, 1951, the High Courts of Orissa and Orissa held that the Act is valid and the notification issued by the Central Government under section 8(1)(a), was invalid. The question whether the said notification is void or non est was not considered by the High courts in the impugned judgment. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 11 of 1951. Appeal from the Judgment and Order dated the 30th July, 1951 of the Orissa High Court in Misc. Case No. 10 of 1950. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, S. N. Andley, J. B. Dadachanji, Rameshwar Nath and P. L. Vohra, for the appellant. A. V. Viswanatha Sastri, R. Ganapathy Iyer, K. R. Chaudhuri, for respondent No. 2. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J.-This appeal is brought on a certificate granted by the Orissa high court under Article 133(1A) of our Constitution against the judgment and order of the High 'Court in writ petition No. 9 of 1950, dated July 30 1951. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant was appointed by the Chief Secretary of the State Government as a Clerk in the Office of the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Orissa on January 31, 1948, and was confirmed in that post on May 22, 1950 by an Order made by the Government of Orissa under section 10(1). On June 29, 1950 he was paid salary at the rate of Rs 10 per month from March 1, 1950 to June 30.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The respondent filed an application for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he was a licensee and not a tenant. The Rent Controller held that the respondent was a sub tenant within the meaning of the Maharashtra Amendment Act 17 of 1973 and that the leave and licence agreement between the parties were renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. The appellant filed an appeal before the District Judge, Bombay. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the revision on the finding that the period of licence had come to an end and in view of the provisions of the [Maharashtra Amendment Act] 17 of 1974, the leave granted by the court was not necessary. In this appeal, it is contended by Mr. S.K. Jain, learned counsel for the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the suit filed by the respondent against the appellants was not maintainable as the leave or licence agreement was not a lease and therefore the leave of the court could not be granted. The question whether the leave was necessary or not was considered by this Court in [D.H. Patel vs State of Gujarat] , wherein it was held that where the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease. The High Court further observed that in view the provisions contained in the Maharashtra amendment Act 17/74 and the Bombay Rent Act, the question whether there was any error apparent on the face of the record does not arise at all. In our opinion, this decision is clearly distinguishable. The facts of this case are different from the facts of the present case. The suit filed against the respondent for eviction was not one for a licence but only a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The leave and Licence agreement between parties were not a mere lease. It was a licence. The period of the licence had came to an implied or licence. In view of this position, we are of the opinion that in the facts and circumstances of this appeal no ground is made out for interference with the decision of the courts below.

The appellant, a former Ruler of the erstwhile State of Jodhpur, was an Indian citizen and had been assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to exemption from payment of income tax in respect of his income from the Mills. The claim was rejected by the Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax on the ground that the appellant had not established that the new State had a right to exempt the Mills from payment income tax. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the Mills had a fundamental right to exemption under the agreement with the Ruler of Jodhpur and that the said rights were available to the Mills only in respect thereof. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the appellant holding that the agreement was not an act of State but was an act done by the new sovereign and therefore, the exemption granted by the agreement could not be enforced against the new Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the agreements were not enforceable against the old Government and that there was no recognition of the rights of the States under the agreements with the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The agreement was an Act of State and was a law. It is true that in view of article VI of the Covenant the exemption in respect to the income from any property in the territory of Jodhpur was granted by this Court. [557 D] 2. The agreements were valid and binding on the new States. The new State could not enforce the rights conferred by the agreements without recognition of those rights. [506 G] 3. The right to apply for exemption under Article VI of Schedule I of the Constitution is a fundamental one and it cannot be enforced in the same way as would have been done if there was any such right. [504 D] 4. The question whether the agreement had been recognised by the old sovereign or not, does not depend upon the continuance of the laws. It depends on the continuance in force of the existing law. [457 H] 5. The rights conferred under the Agreement were not an enforceable right but only a legal right and therefore they could be enforced only against the State. [500 D] 6. The provisions of the agreement were not intended to be enforced by the State legislature or the new state. The terms of the agreements did not contemplate that there must be recognition by the Union of the right to exemptions, if any, under the Agreements with the Rulers of the former Jodhpur State. The Agreement was not a law and therefore it could not have been enforced against it. [511 D] 7. The fact that the Agreement was an order passed by the Government of Rajasthan in exercise of its powers under Article V of the covenant does not affect the rights which were available under the contract to the appellant for exemption from tax. [556 G] 8. The application of the provisions of Article VI is a law made by the competent legislature and cannot be regarded as an act or deed of State. It was not necessary that there should be recognition of such rights in the agreement. [558 H] 9. The conditions mentioned in the agreements are not enforceable by the States. They were not merely contracts which could be entered into by the Ruler but were also contracts which were executed by the Rulers themselves and they were not binding on them. [560 G] 10. The State legislature was competent to make laws for the purpose of securing that the rights granted under the covenant were not affected by the provisions contained in Article VI. [561 H] 11. The power to grant exemption from taxation is a right conferred by Article VI and it can be enforced even against the Government. [562 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1971. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1970 of the Rajasthan High Court in S. T. C. No. 11 of 1969. M. C.. Agarwala, for the appellant (in C.A. 13/71).

The appellants, who were the members of the market committee, were carrying on business in cotton and cotton seeds. They purchased cotton from the market for a price of Rs. 1,000 per acre. The market committee assessed the market fee to be paid by the appellants under section 14(1)(b) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the market committees did not have any power to levy tax on the sale of cotton and that the said amount was not a trade allowance but a trade allowances. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 14 (1)(a), the said sum was not deductible from the price or commodity agreed to be sold by the market Committee. On the question whether 'mahimai' is a trade or not, the learned Judges held that it was not necessary for the appellants to prove that they were entitled to do business in the market and that they had no power to impose tax on sale of goods. The appellants filed appeals against the said decision to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 14(l)(a) and 14(2) are not exhaustive and they cannot be read as a whole. [675 H] 2. Section 14(3) of Act is an exception to section 14 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 which provides that no tax shall be payable by any dealer on his sale of any goods specified in Schedule I or Schedule II unless he has paid the tax under that Schedule. The said provision does not make it obligatory for the Market Committees to pay tax on purchase of cotton. [775 H; 776 A] 3. Section 15(1) of Central Sales Act, which provides for deduction of trade allowance and other deductions is a general provision and it is not necessary to prove whether the said provisions are exhaustive or not. The fact that 'maajai' was a trading asset does not mean that the Market Committee did not pay tax under section 15(2). [776 H] 4. Section 16(1), as amended by Act No. 1 of 1976, is an exemption from payment of trade allowances and it cannot be said that the provisions contained in section 14 are exhaustive and do not apply to a case where 'maajan' is not a trading assets. [750 A] 5. The question whether the Market committees did have power to tax the sale or purchase of goods does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [751 H] 6. Section 17(1A) of C.P.C. provides that the amount payable by the Market committee under section 16 shall be a trade discount and shall be paid on such price or commodities as may be specified by the State Government. The proviso to section 17(2), however, does not apply in this case because the said provision is an exempting provision and the said clause does not cover the case of a trader. [753 H] 7. Section 18(1B) of A.P.(C) No. 15 of 1976 is an instance of discrimination against a trader or a person who is not registered under section 17. The Market Committees do not have power under section 18 to impose any tax on their sale of the goods specified therein. [764 H] 8. Section 19(1-A) provides that in case of sale of agricultural produce, the seller shall be liable to pay trade discounts and other charges as may from time to time be specified. The Explanation to section 19(2)(b), however does not exclude the said item from the purview of section 15. [774 H; 771 A] 9. Section 20 provides that a trader who is registered under the Act shall be entitled to trade discount on his turnover in respect of any sale of his produce.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for murder of one Ramchander and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence, the appellant was found in possession of a large number of articles and he was found guilty of having committed an offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was also found guilty for having committed murder of Ramchader. The trial court convicted him for the offence of murder and sentenced him to death, but acquitted him of the charge under Section 376 of the Code. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant. In this Court, it was contended that in view of section 377 of the code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code") the appellant should have been given a chance to show that he was a person who had committed an act which would be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and that the sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not be convicted for murder under Section 377 read with [Section 34] of the Penal Code unless he had a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against his conviction. [557 D] 2. In the present case, the prosecution case is that on account of the appellant's conduct, he was guilty of committing an offence which would not be prejudicial or injurious to public order. The question whether he should be given a hearing or not is a matter of discretion and such discretion has to be exercised by the Judges in this behalf. [506 D] 3. In view of the provisions contained in Section 377 of Code, it is not necessary for the prosecution to show any cause against an act done by the accused who had been found guilty. The fact that the accused was a young man and that he had committed the offence would be relevant under section 377 read along with section 34 of Indian Penal code. [504 D] 4. In considering whether there is a reasonable probability of the commission of an offence, it has to see whether the law requires such proof. If the law provides for an inference of common intention in that behalf, it can be safely presumed that the act was done by accused who was found not guilty. [500 G] 5. The conviction and the sentence passed against the appellant is liable to be set aside. [511 D] 6. In a case where the evidence discloses no cause for an act of murder, the Court has discretion to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons. [54 H] 7. The power under section 378 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not exercised in the interests of public justice and it is necessary that the law should be so read as not to exceed its limits. [55 D] 8. In dealing with a case involving an offence under Section 304, the Constitution Bench held that the Court must consider whether there was a reasonable possibility of the crime. The Court has to consider whether the circumstances in which the offence was committed were such that it would be safe for the Judge to impose death penalty irrespective of the fact that he is a young person and if he is found guilty, then the sentence of death should not be imposed. [56 D] 9. In determining whether there are any compelling reasons, the court has to take into consideration all the circumstances which are in favour of the accused. The court must consider all the facts and circumstances in order to determine whether it would not impose the capital punishment unless the circumstances of the case justify such imposition. [57 F] 10. The decision of this Court in [South India Match Co.] vs State of Punjab, referred to. 11. In deciding whether there were any compelling circumstances, the Judge has to apply his mind to the facts of each case and then come to a conclusion as to whether the accused is guilty of murder under Sections 302/34 of the IPC.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Central Public Works Department in the year 1962 and they were promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on ad hoc basis. They were confirmed in the post in the scale of Rs. 700-1050/- with effect from 1st April, 1966. The petitioners were promoted as Assistant Engineer in the pay scale of `700-1060/-. On their promotion to the higher post they were appointed to the said post by direct recruitment and were confirmed on ad d hoc basis on a regular basis. The petitioner was promoted as Executive Engineer in Class I or Class II service or post on officiating basis. He was promoted to that post on ad vance of Rule 56(j) (i) of the Rules. On his promotion to that grade he was reverted to the substantive post and was not entitled to any salary and allowances for the period from 1 st April, 1967 to 31st March, 1968. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court held that the petitioner had no right to hold the post as Assistant Executive Engineer and he was not liable to be reverted to his substantive post before the expiry of the period of probation. It was further held that Rule 56 (j) was applicable to the case and the petitioner was entitled to salary and other service allowances payable to him from the date of compulsory retirement till the date o f his normal superannuation. The writ petition filed by the petitioners was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Rule 56 is not attracted to the facts of the case as it does not apply to the cases of promotion or reversion of a person to the service or grade in which he has been promoted. [690B] 1.2 The ratio of the decision in Tahiliani's case is not applicable to Government servants in Class II or Class III service or posts on substantive, temporary or offi cient basis. [650C] 1:3. Rule 56 does not come into play as it applies to Government servant who at the relevant time was in Class 11 service or a post on substantive appointment. The ratio in Tahilani's cases is not correct and therefore the petitioner cannot be reverted back to his original post. [790D] 2.1 The ratio laid down in Tahriliani's case is applicable to cases of reversion of an employee to the regular post. Rule56(j)(i) does not cover Government servants who at any time were in Class III or Class IV service or Post or post, whether substantively or officiating or on officiating or temporary basis. Therefore, the petitioner's appointment as Assistant Engineee was not a promotion and he could be reverted from that post to his regular post only if he had been promoted to officiate in the substantive capacity. [750D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 851 of 1981. From the Judgment and Order dated the 14th July, 1973 of the High court of Judicature at Allahabad in Writ Petition No. 1252 of 1972. S.K. Sinha, for the appellant. R. K. Garg, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 14th August, 1973 passed by the High,Court at Allahabad dismissing the writ petition. The appellant was appointed as a Assistant Engineer on probation in Class-III service or in the regular cadre or post and he joined the said service on officiating capacity. He had been confirmed on the post on probation for a period of two years from 1.4.1966 to 31.3.1968. On the basis of this confirmation, he was promoted on ad-hoc basis as Executive Engineers on officiating appointment. On promotion to higher post, he became eligible for promotion to officiate as Executive engineer on officiating appointments.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India, the appellant, filed a petition under Section 7 of the Act before the District Judge, Delhi, for an order directing the respondents to pay the amount covered by the insurance policy. The deceased was employed as a driver in the respondent-Corporation. He died on November 11, 1966. The respondent filed a claim for compensation claiming Rs. 1,00,000/and interest at the rate of 18% per annum from the date of death till payment. The appellant contended that the deceased was not entitled to any amount under the policy and therefore he was not liable to pay any amount. The District Judge held that the respondent was entitled to a sum of Rs. 2,007/and awarded interest at 18% p.a. On appeal by the Life Insurance corporation, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the District Court. The High Court also directed the appellant to pay interest at 9% p., on the amount paid under the insurance policies. The Corporation filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 The respondent was not an employee of the Corporation and he was entitled only to the payment of the first premium. [775D] 1.2 The High court was right in holding that there was a concluded contract between the deceased and the Life insurance Corporation. The liability of the Life insured under the Insurance Policy was limited to Rs. 50,000/- and not to Rs 2,50,000/-. [776F] 1:3. The question whether the respondent is entitled to interest at 12% p,.a. on the amounts paid by the deceased for the first time in this case does not arise in this appeal. [750D] 2.1 There was a valid insurance policy between the parties and the respondent had no liability to pay compensation. The Life Insurance Corpn. of India is the only authority competent to accept the proposal and it cannot be said that there is a concluded agreement between the Corporation or the Life assured. [751F] 2:2. In the instant case, the deceased died on December 11, 1967 and he had no interest in the amount payable under the terms of the policy. He was not a member of the family of the deceased. The death of the respondent occurred on November 10, 1966 and he is entitled only for the payment to the extent of Rs 2 lakhs. [753F] 3.2 In the facts and circumstances of this case there will be no order as to costs in this Appeal.

The appellant was a Company, which owned the property of one B. S. Agarwal. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of income tax dues on the basis that the property in question was owned by B.S. Agarwal and that the appellant had obtained an order from the Court of Small Causes, Bombay, to sell the property. The respondent filed a written statement contending that the suit was not maintainable as the plaintiff had no right to recover the income tax due from the property and that he was entitled to recover income tax arrears on the ground that the order passed by the High Court in appeal was an interlocutory order within the meaning of article 133 (1) (c). The trial court held that the respondent was entitled, as a result of the order of the High court, to recover his income tax from the properties and that it was not open to the appellant to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief. On appeal by the respondent, the High, Court reversed the decree passed by both the trial court and the first appellate court. The High Court held that in view of section 109 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the order made by the Court was an interim order within (1)(2) E.L.R. 1958 S.C.R., The appellant preferred a second appeal to this Court. HELD: 1. The provisions of article 134(1) are not applicable to the present case as the suit is not maintainable. [975 H] 2. The order passed in appeal by a learned Single Judge of the Bombay High Court was not an interlocutory one and, therefore, the appellant could not seek amendment to get appropriate relief. [999 G] 3. The question whether an order passed under section 205 read with section 114 I.P. Code can be said to be final for the purposes of article 136 does not arise in this case as it is not a case where the plaintiff has no right or obligation to determine the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit. [991 H] 4. The expression "final order" in section 109 means an interlocutory orders within the scope of article 137. [1075 G] 5. In the instant case, the trial Court was wrong in holding that the application filed by the appellant under section 208 read with sections 114 and 114 I,P.C., was not a suit as contemplated by article 134 (1). [999 H] 6. The appeal is allowed. The judgment of the learned Single judge is set aside and the suit filed by respondent No. 1 is dismissed.

The price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. The cost of the processing be allowed by the Excise authorities as per Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 346.The price of grey cloth or fabric plus the value of the processed fabrics plus the cost of job work plus the manufacturer's profit. The price at the factory gate for the processed fabric would include both the price at that time and the processing profit and manufacturing expenses. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would either be post manufacturing profits or manufacturing expenses, but not an independent subsequent profit and cost of processing plus the price thereof. The manufacturer's profits and manufacturing costs are required to be included in the price under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The prices at which they were sold by the processor to the fabric plus his profit. It is necessary to include only such price or deemed price at any other relevant profit and expenses. It was further stated that the declared price at factory gate would include all the cost, manufacturing profit, manufacturing expenses and manufacturing profit. In the case of cotton cloth or manmade fabrics, the processor was selling the grey cloth in the hands of the processor. The processor was paying duty on the processed cloth as per the provisions of the Act and Rules. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. On further appeal to the Tribunal, it upheld the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner. In second appeal before this Court, the Revenue contended that the processor had not paid duty on grey cloth as required under the provisions contained in Section 11A of the 1944 Act and Rule 174 read with Rule 173B of the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right in holding that the price charged by the manufacturer to the processing partner for processing the processed cotton fabrics would include the processor 's expenses' and the cost thereof. [532E] 2.1 The price charged under Section 11 A of the Excise Act is the price which the assessee is selling the goods. It does not include the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be postmanufacturing profit. [633F] 2:2 In the instant case, the price was at factory rate and the processor did not pay duty on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price is required to the manufacturer. The declared price was Rs.20 and the job worked profit and Rs.5,000/- were job work charges. [650F] 3.1 In order that the assessable value of grey fabrics should be taken into account, it must include all cost, including the trader's profit and in addition the manufacturing profits and the selling profit. If the declared prices at factory or gate for processing are not included in price under Section11A of Excise Act, the manufacturer would be entitled to take out the goods from the market. [663F] 4.1 There is no material on record to show that the assessee had paid duty as per provisions contained under Section 3(a) of the said act. The fact that the trader was selling processed cotton cloth in his own factory for processing does not mean that he would have been selling the fabrics in the open market. He has only sold the grey fabric in the wholesale trade and the price paid by him to the process partner for the processing is not a part of the cost or manufacturing profit but it is a part thereof. It cannot be said that the manufacturer had not discharged his duty liability as per Section 11-A of Central Excise Act. [664F] 5. The assessee was selling grey cloth and he was selling it in the same market.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti, on an ad hoc basis. He was promoted as a head clerk on an adhoc basis in 1963 and he was confirmed in that post on June 13, 1973. The appellant was promoted to the post of a Headman on an officiating basis on April 1, 1975. On July 14, 1975, the Government issued an order appointing the appellant as a Sub-Inspector of Police with effect from April 1. 1975. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging his appointment as a sub-inspector of police. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to be considered for promotion on a regular basis. The State Government, however, issued an amendment to the Amending Act by which the appellant's appointment as Sub- Inspector of Police was withdrawn. The effect of the amendment was that the appointment of the appellant to the said post was made after June 13 1975 when the Amending act came into force. The question whether the appellant should be considered as a member of the Panchayat Samiti or not was not raised in the writ proceedings before the High court. The learned Single Judge held that the right to be heard and to be treated as a term and condition of service, was a term. The Division Bench also held that there was no substance in this contention. The appeal filed by the appellant against the judgment of the learned Single judge was dismissed by the Division Bench. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 The right to hold the post as a whole is a term, and condition for the appointment to the service is an element and condition. [775 H] 1.2 The appellant should have been considered for being considered for such promotion on regular basis by the Government. He should be absorbed in the Government service. [750 A] 1:3 The right of the respondent to be promoted as Head Clerk was a condition of his appointment with effect form April 1 1975 and he could not be treated to be a member thereof. [751 B] 1 Whether the right of promotion is a condition or condition of the service, it has to be decided by the State Government in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The right conferred on the respondent under section 14(4) of the Amending Ordinance was a statutory right and could not have been taken away by the Legislature.

The respondent, a managing corporation of the appellant company, was allotted a plot of land in the area of village Kothra, District Ambala, by the Central Government under the provisions of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The appellant company had been allotted a piece of land measuring about 2 acres in village Kanjara, District Karnal, for construction of a house thereon. On March 24, 1955, the Central government issued an order under section 12(1) of the Act directing that the respondent should be allotted a site at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per acre. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and praying for a direction to the appellant to allot him a site in village Dhandi, District Faridabad, and also for a declaration that the allotment made by the respondent was illegal. The High Court held that the land allotted to the respondent did not belong to the Central Govt., and that the appellant was entitled to the relief claimed. It further directed that the amount of compensation payable to the displaced person should be paid to him within one month from the date of the order. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court was in error in holding that section 12 of the 1954 Act did not apply to the case and that section 19(1)(f) of that Act did apply to a case where the allotment was made in favour of a displaced person. [757 D] (ii) Section 19(2) of this Act does not apply in the case of a transfer by the Government of any property in the compensation pool entrusted to him or it. The provisions of section 12 are clear and unambiguous. It is not necessary for the purpose of determining whether section 19 of the 1955 Act applies to a transfer made in contravention of section 19. [857 D C] (iii) Section 12(2)(a) does not cover a case of transfer by an allottee to another person. The question whether section 12 is attracted only in a case when the allotment is made in his favour does not arise for consideration in this case. The fact that the property allotted to respondent was not acquired by the appellant or it was used or is used by him for a purpose other than that for which it was allotted did not make any difference to the question whether the transfer was made by him in contravention with section 19 or not. [957 D E] (iv) Section 13(1A) of Act No. 1 of 1956 does not affect the power of the Custodian General under section 11 of the 1952 Act. The property allotted by the Custodian is not a evacuee property and therefore, it cannot be said that section 9 of the 1953 Act applies in the present case to a transaction which was not done by the custodian or any other person. Section 13 (1A), therefore, does not operate as res judicata against the appellant. [1057 D F] (v) The question of cancellation of allotment is not relevant for the purposes of section 11 and the High court erred in holding otherwise. The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. They were promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on October 29, 1979 and they were promoted as Executive Engineers on November 30, 1979. The petitioners were promoted on December 31, 1980 and they had completed their probation period of service from December 1, 1980 to January 31, 1981. On March 28, 1982, the Government issued a notification in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. The question as regards the age of retirement was considered by this Court in [State of Punjab vs. Amar Singh] and Ors., [1983] 1 SCC 305. In that case, the State Government had reduced the age from 55 to 58 years. The High Court held that the reduction of the age was not justified. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 is a power which is exercised by the President in exercise or revision of powers conferred on him under Article 311 read with Articles 14 and 16. [775 H] (2) The proviso to clause (1)(a) of Article 309 provides that the President may, if he considers it necessary or expedient so to do, make rules for carrying out the purposes of the said article. The proviso does not confer any power on the Government to alter the conditions of service of a person who is promoted on the basis of his own pay scale. [750 H] In the instant case, there was no provision in the proviso which empowered the Government either to reduce or reduce the age. The power to reduce the retirement age was exercised by this court in exercise o the powers under Article 309 and Article 313 read with Section 2(1)(c) of the Act. [751 A] (3) The High Courts were right in holding that the proviso did not confer a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of services. [75 H; 75 B] (4) The provision for reduction of age was made by the Government under Article 310 read with clause (2)(a). The power of the President to alter or reduce retirement age is not exercised by him in exercise, of the power conferred on the President under Article 162 read with Clause (1), clause (3).

The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Sales tax Officer. On further appeal to the Tribunal, it held that there was no material on record to justify the conclusion that the purchase was not made by the purchasing dealers in the goods purchased by them from the buyers at Bombay. The Tribunal also held that though the purchasingdealer had declared the goods as "a registered dealer" he did not make a false statement in the Certificate issued by him and that therefore the purchasing Dealer was liable to pay purchase tax on the purchase of the goods.
