The appellant was married to the respondent on April 1, 1962. The marriage between the parties took place on December 31, 1961. The respondent filed a petition under section 125 of the Code for maintenance and the trial court passed an order directing the respondent to pay maintenance at the rate of Rs. 500/- per month. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the order of the trial judge. In further appeal to this Court it was contended that the marriage between her and the respondent was not a valid marriage as defined in section 125(3) (b). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether a wife is entitled to maintenance under section 127(3)(b) or not must be determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [675 H] 2. The object of the payment by way of mehar money was to ensure that the woman was given full opportunity to maintain herself. The provision for maintenance was a social obligation by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. [775 H; 776 B] 3. The provisions of section 127 (3) are manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the party. The purpose of the Payment Order was to provide for the divorcee and the husband was not entitled to claim under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties. [750 H] 4. The expression 'under any customary, personal law' in section 127 is a comprehensive expression which includes the provision for the maintenance of wife and the provision of the personal laws of the other party. [751 G] 5. The word 'under" used in section 126(3), means that the payment should be made by way or under any custom. The words "by a customary or special form of marriage" are not intended to convey the idea that no husband can claim maintenance under any special statute. [751 H] 6. The scheme of section 125 is manifestly to recognize the substitute Maintenance arrangement by the terms of the marriage and it is not necessary for the wife to make out a case under section 126. [764 G] 7. The language of section 126 is clear and unambiguous. It does not require that any husband can be entitled to get maintenance under the provisions of the Act. [754 H] 8. The payment by the respondent in terms of an agreement to pay 'under some customary or other form of a marriage, is a social duty by the Court. The obligation to provide maintenance to the wife is a statutory right and not a personal law. [752 G] 9. The section does not contemplate that any person can claim under section 128(3). [754 H] 10. The proviso to section 127 makes it clear that no wife can claim as of right maintenance under an agreement for maintenance under which the husband is entitled under the Hindu Law to get a maintenance under such a custom. [758 G] 11. Section 127(1) does not make any provision for payment of maintenance to a divorced wife. The only restriction on the ground of desertion and absence of any other provision in the Act is that no person can be deprived of his right to claim maintenance by reason of the provisions contained in section 128. [759 H] 12. Section 126(1)(b), therefore, does not create an obligation on the husband to provide a wife for maintenance. The appellant, the respondent, was a tenant of a building in the city of Madras. The appellant let out a portion of the building to the respondent on rent for a period of five years and paid a monthly rent of Rs.5,000/- to the landlord. On the expiry of the lease, the landlord filed an application under section 4 of the Act before the Rent Controller for fixation of fair rent in respect of the entire building. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 64 C. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court and the High court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Rent Control Court and remanded the case to the Rent Tribunal for deciding it afresh in accordance with law. On remand, the Rent Appellate Authority held that the relationship of landlord and tenant was not established between the parties and accordingly, the rent was fixed by the Rent Authority. The High Court also held that since the appellant had failed to establish his claim of title over the entire property, the question of exclusion of a civil court 's jurisdiction did not arise at all. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts' decision in regard to the exclusion of civil courts' s jurisdiction was erroneous and should be set aside. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the Rent Act does not apply to the facts of the case because the question whether the appellant is a tenant or not, has to be decided by the authorities concerned. It is further contended that the question as to the applicability of section 4 C.P.C. was not considered by the High courts and, therefore, the decision in the earlier proceedings should not be interfered with. The question whether there was relationship of a landlord and a tenant between the appellant and the respondent was decided by this Court in [R.K. Jain vs Union of India & Ors.] , ; , ; (i) that the issue as to whether the relationship was established between parties, was not decided by any authority other than the Rent control authorities; (ii) that, therefore. the question regarding applicability of Section 64 C was not raised before the High C Court and, on a proper interpretation of the provisions of the said Act, it was held that there is no merit in the appeal. The point for consideration is whether the High-Court has erred in law in holding that there was a relationship of the landlord and the tenant between them. The relevant provision of section 2(4) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, which reads as follows: "2.(4). A landlord shall not be entitled to recover possession of any building under this Act on the ground that it is an arrear of rent."

The petitioner submitted his reply to the charge-sheets on April 30 and June 1967. On May 29, 1967 the petitioner was served a memorandum of charges under Rule 10 of the Rules. He pleaded not guilty to the charges but stated that he was guilty of the offence charged against him. The disciplinary authority after considering the evidence adduced by the parties held that the petitioner had been proved guilty of an offence charged with misconduct in relation to his conduct and that he should be given a reasonable opportunity to make a representation against the proposed penalty upon the findings of the enquiry officer. On June 30, 1968 the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the disciplinary authority. The High Court held that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice and accordingly quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the disciplinary authorities was not vitiated on any ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list was absent, inasmuch as the Central Government had acted properly according to the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The order of suspension dated April 30 1967 is liable to be quashed on this ground alone. [775 H] 2. The appellant has been given a fair opportunity to show cause against the alleged misconduct and he was afforded an adequate opportunity to meet the charges. [750 A] 3. Rule 10(1) of the rules provides that if a Government servant is dismissed or removed from service, he shall be given reasonable opportunity of making representation against such order. The provisions of Rule 10 (1) are mandatory in nature and it cannot be said that the disciplinary proceedings were vitiated on this account. [751 B] 4. The principles of justice demand that an employee should be afforded a reasonable hearing before any action is taken against him, but the same cannot be done without giving him an opportunity to explain his conduct. [751 D] 5. The rules do not provide for any procedure for the purpose of holding an enquiry into the charges framed against the petitioner. Rule 9(2) provides that where a Government Servant is dismissed, removed or reduced in rank on the basis of misconduct as a result of which he was found guilty, he should also be given an adequate reasonable opportunity before any penalty is imposed upon him. [764 D] 6. The rule does not provide that if the disciplinary proceeding was initiated against the Government servant, he could have been given an opportunity of showing cause against such action. [754 G] 7. Rule 11 provides for a hearing to be given to the petitioner and it is not open to the disciplinary/appellate authority to go behind the rules. [752 B] 8. The procedure prescribed by the Rules is mandatory in character and it does not require any interference with the order under appeal. [758 C] 9. Rule 12 provides that the appellate authority shall give an opportunity for hearing to the appellant before passing orders on the appeal. The appellate authority has no power to go into the merits of the case or otherwise interfere with the findings recorded by the enquiry Officer. [759 D] 10.

The petitioners imported raw materials and components from the Government of India, Ministry of Commerce, New Delhi. They were granted Additional licences under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 for the period from April 1, 1985 to March 31, 1988. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the said Additional licences on the ground that they had been granted Additional Licences under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947 and were entitled to import raw materials as per the Import Policy 1978-79. The High Court held that the petitioners were entitled for the extension of the period of the Additional licences which have been granted to them under the said Import & Exports Policy 1978 81. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Additional Licences issued by the Government under the import and export policy 1978 79 were valid for a period of twelve months from the date of such extension and, therefore, they were entitled only to the benefit of the additional licences granted to the petitioners under the Export & Import Policy 1979 81. The respondents contended that the said licences were valid till March 31. 1988 and, as such, they could not be denied the benefit on the basis of the expiry of the original period of 12 months from April 1985 to May 1986. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to the extension in terms of the Import and Export Policy 1979 79. [557F] 1.2 The petitioners were granted additional licences under Import & Import policy 1978 81 for the periods from April, 1985 onwards. The period of validity of Additional Licences was extended by six months from that date. The said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. [546G] 1:3. The question whether the period for which the Additional Licence is granted to Export Houses under the Exports and Import Policy 1980 79 should be extended by a period longer than 12 months, does not arise in this case because the petitioners had been given Additional licences for a further period of six months. The extension of period of licence was not extended by the said period. [547G] 2.1 There is no provision in the Import Control Policy 197879 for grant of additional licences to Export House under the Customs and Import & Exim Policy 1979 80. [548A G] 1 Whether the petitioners are similarly circumstanced as Export Houses, whether they were granted extension of time or not, is a question of fact which has to be decided by the Court. The Additional Licences granted to these petitioners under Import and Exports Policy 1980 81 have expired during pendency of this writ petition. [549F] 2:2 There was no provision for grant extension of such period. The licences were issued to the petitioner under the provisions of the Export and Import and Exim policy 1979 79 as amended by the Import, Export Policy 1981 80. The petitioner had been denied the extension on the plea that the period during which the additional licence was granted to him under the Additional licence was extended. [556F] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioners have not challenged the validity and the period between April 1985 and May 1986 and they were not entitled to any relief on the said ground. The writ petitions are therefore dismissed.

The assessee, a manufacturer of the drums and packing materials, filed a return under section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for the assessment year 1964-65. The assessing authority assessed the cost of the packing material at Rs. 1,50,000/- and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 50,000/-. On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that the cost incurred by the assessee was not includible in the assessable value of the goods for the purpose of assessment. The High Court further held that as the packing materials were supplied by the buyer to the assessee, the cost thereof would be included in the price and accordingly, the value of such packing material was liable to be included. On appeal by the Revenue, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the High court and held that since the cost was incurred by a manufacturer on account of the cost which was not incurred by him, the assessee is entitled to claim deduction under section 5(2)(d) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the cost should be included or not in the value for the purposes of assessment is a question of fact and it cannot be decided in this case on the basis of the facts and circumstances of the case. [775 H] 1.2 In the instant case, as the assessee had supplied the drums to the buyer, the price was required to be added to the assessable values for determining the value. The cost of packing was not a part of the assessable price but was a part thereof. Therefore, the question whether it should be taken into account in arriving at the assessable amount did not arise. [750 H] 2.1 In the present case, the manufacturer had supplied drums and charges the customers separately therefore, the expenses incurred by them were includible in their assessable value. [751 G] 2:2 The cost incurred for packing of the containers was not deductible under section 11(4) of Central Excise Act, 1944. [753 H] 3.1 There is no merit in the contention that the costs of packing are includible in assessable value and accordingly the question of deduction does not arise at all. [752 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1579 of 1989. From the Judgment and Order dated 2.2.1989 of the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT), New Delhi in Appeal No.. C/875/89-D. V.S. Desai, S.K. Bagaria, R.K Jain, M.M. The appeal against this order was dismissed by the Appellate Collector of Central Excises and Customs, Bombay. Hence this appeal. 2. Shri S. K. The appellant was a member of the Punjab National Bank, who had been working as an Assistant Manager in the Bank. He was prosecuted for offences under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The trial court convicted him of the offence under section 6 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The High Court, however, confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that clause (d) of section 5 (1) of Prevention of corruption Act is not attracted because the explanation offered by the appellant was reasonable and probable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The presumption under section 4(1) is a rebuttable one. It must further be shown that the explanation is a true one. [675 H] 2. Clause (d), clause (e) of sub-section (1), of section 6, provides that on being proved to have been guilty of an offence punishable under section 5 or section 6 he shall be liable to suffer rigorous imprisonment which may extend to three years and fine. The explanation is not exhaustive. It only says that the accused person has received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration. [775 H; 776 A] 3. Clause(d) clause (f) of subsection (1A) of Section 5, provides for an additional presumption that the person receiving the amount of money is the receipt of any gratification other than legal remuneration and cannot be said to have received such thing as a motive of reward such as is mentioned in section 161, I. P.C., or section 5 of the [Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1976]. [776 H] 4. Clause 2(d), (e), (f), (g) and (h) of clause (1)(a) are not attracted when the explanation given by the accused is reasonable and the explanation being a true statement made by him. The Explanation to section 5 makes it clear that on proof of the fact that the said explanation was reasonable, the court has no option but to draw a presumption that such person had received a monetary gratification other then legal remuneration or any valuable thing as is referred to in section 6. [750 H] 5. Clause 3(d)(i) of Schedule I of the Code provides for a presumption of guilt under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot therefore be said that clause 2(e), clause 2 (f). [778 A] 6. The words "any gratification other" in clause (g), clause 4(2), clause 5(1)(e) and clause (h), clause 3(i) are wide enough to include the acceptance of a monetary sum by a person as a consideration for a transaction which is not punishable under clauses (d). [750 B] 7. Clause 6(a) of schedule I of Preventionof Corruption Act provides that if the accused has received any gratification as a reward other than a legal tender, or any kind of gratification other in connection with the receipt thereof, such gratification shall be deemed to have given and received by the court. The expression "any amount" in clauses (e). [751 H] 8. Clause 4(3) of Article 20 of the Constitution provides that no person accused of an act specified in clause(d). or clause (i) is attracted when a person has been convicted of an offense punishable under clause (a), clause 1(b). [751 A] 9. The word "any" in the context means "any sum" as defined in section 5. [751 B] 10. Clause 7(d)-A gratification other that is mentioned therein does not include a consideration which is the one mentioned in clause 2 of Article 19 of the constitution. [753 H] 11.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the company on January 1, 1957. He was appointed by the company as an officer of the company. On December 31, 1959, he was transferred to the State Bank of India, Bombay and was posted at Bombay. On June 30, 1960, he served with a notice under section 630 of the Act for recovery of his dues from the company in respect of the period from January 1. 1961 to March 31, 1962. The appellant filed a suit against the company for recovery on the ground that the property in question was held by him as an employee of the Company and not as a tenant of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the property from the respondent. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and directed the trial court to deliver the property back to the company and to pay the amount due to it. It also held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 631 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The respondent filed a second appeal before this Court. HELD: (i) Section 630 of The Act does not apply to the property of a company as defined in section 630(1)(b). [675 H] (ii) The words "any such property" used in cl. (a) of sub section (1) of section 630, namely, 'any such properties' used in clause (b), are referable to the whole of cl. Jagtiani vs Sirajuddin section Kazi, (supra). [775 H; 776 A] (iii) The word 'any' used by the legislature in sub section 2 of section 631 must be construed as a reference to the entire of cl.(a) and not to any other part of cl (b). The words 'any other part' used both in cl.(b) and in cl(b) are meant to refer to the remaining part of the clause. [776 H] In the instant case, the appellant had been given a right to recover the amount from the Company after the termination of his employment. [750 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1124 of 1967. This appeal by special Leave is directed against the judgment dated September 29, 1966 passed by the High court of Bombay in Special civil Application No 826/65. The facts leading to this appeal are as follows: The appellant was employed as an Assistant Manager in the Company on January 31, 1957 and was transferred from the State of Bombay to the Government of India. On July 1, 1960 he served on the respondent a notice of recovery under section 6 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for recovery from the appellant in respect thereof. The notice was served on him on June 30. 1961 and he filed his written statement on August 29, 1960. On September 30. 1962 the appellant filed an application under section 7 of the said Act for a certificate that the notice was not served on it. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the service of the notice on the appellant could be deemed to have been effected by the respondent in accordance with law. Accordingly, the certificate issued by the Income Tax Officer was quashed and the appellant's application was dismissed. The appellant was the Mahant of a temple in the year 1932. He was appointed as a manager by the then Ruler of the State of Bombay. The appellant was appointed a Manager of the temple and he was to manage the affairs of the said temple. On his appointment, he was appointed an Assistant Commissioner of Endowments, Madras, for the management of the properties of the deity. The trustees of the trust were appointed as members of the public in respect of the lands belonging to the temple. The respondents filed a suit against the appellant and the appellant in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, First Class, Amalner, for a declaration that the said properties were not private property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties were public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the appellant was a public trust and he could not be treated as a public religious endowment within the definition of section 3(1)(b) of Act No. 1 of 1951. The High Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 4 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950, the properties belonging to an idol were not public trust property. On further appeal by special leave, the Court HELD: (i) The properties in question were public religious endowments within the scope of section 6 of the General Clauses Act and therefore they were private properties within the purview of section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act. [775 H] (ii) The High court was right in holding that there was no evidence to warrant that a property was a private trust within section 2 of the aforesaid Act. The fact that the temple was not public religious Endowment within the ambit of section 8 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1951, does not affect the question whether the appellant is a public or a religious endowment. [750 H] In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed as Manager by the Ruler of Bombay and he had been managing the affairs in perpetuity. The temple was an integral part of the family. The properties belonging thereto were not dedicated to any religious purpose. The question whether a property is a private or public trust does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [751 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1152 of 1966. Appeal by special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 9th July, 1967 of the High court of Bombay in Writ Petition No. 8 of 1965. S. T. Desai, R. N. Sachthey and B. D. Sharma for the Appellant. V. M. Tarkunde, K. L. Hathi and P. C. Kapur for Respondent No. 2. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. This appeal is directed against a judgment of the Madras High Court dated September 9, 1967 in Writ Appeal No.. 8 of 1966 whereby the High Courts' order dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant has been set aside and the writ petitioner has been held to be a public institution within the provisions contained in section 2 (13) read with section 5(1) of Hindu Religious Endowment Act, and therefore it is not necessary for us to go into the question as to whether the properties belong to an individual or a public body. The facts leading up to this appeal are that the respondents filed an application before the Subordinate Court, Amallur, under section 4 read with [section 5(2)] of the Public Trust (Amendment) Act, 1967, for setting aside the order passed by the High-Court in the writ proceedings. The said application was dismissed on the ground that the property belonged to an institution which was not a public one within the mischief of section 12 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act. It is not disputed that the trust was not registered under section 5 (1) readwith section 5. The appeal therefore fails and it is accordingly dismissed.

The Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 13(1) of the Constitution. The Bombay City Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 (hereinafter referred to as "the Bombay City Act") was enacted by the Central Legislature and it received the assent of the President on the 8th June, 1888. Section 46(2) of that Act provided for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in which they were liable to pay land revenue or any other sum payable under a single Central Act. The State Government issued a notification dated the 7th June 1955 under section 46(1), declaring that the Bombay City Civil Court had jurisdiction over the area in which the Bombay city was situated and that the provisions of the Bombay Municipal Corporation (Amendment) Act, 1955 were applicable to all cases where they were not liable to be detained for a period of more than one year. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued by the Government under section 16(1). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State legislature had no competence to enact the Bombay Act and that it was competent to pass an order under section 13 of the said Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 46 of the Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Ordinance, 1956 provided for detention of defaulters for a longer period than one month in all other cases in all States. The provisions of section 46 were applicable only to those classes of defaulters who had not paid up the Union demand as required by section 46 and that section was not applicable to them. [775 H] (ii) Section 16(2)(a) of Bombay City Improvement Act, 1911 did not apply to cases where the arrears of land revenue were not payable in all the States. It only provided for a different period of time for recovery of all dues. The provision of section 16 was applicable to cases in respect of which the provisions were applicable. [750 H] In the instant case, the State Government had no jurisdiction to enact an order of arrest under section 7 of the Act. [751 G] (iii) Section 17(2), as amended by the Bombay Town Planning and Development Act, 1957 provided for an order made by the Collector under section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The power to make an order was conferred on the State. The notification issued under section 4 of the Gujarat City Improvement Trust Act, 1962 was not a valid notification. [753 H] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition Nos. 858 and 859 of 1972. (Under Article 32 of the constitution) AND WRIT PETITION No. 862 of 1972 (Under article 32 of Constitution) AND CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 952-954 OF 1972 (From the judgment and order dated the 17th September, 1971 of the High court of Bombay in Writ Petition No. 1258 of 1972). M.C. Bhandare, S.K. Mehta, V.M. Tarkunde, K.S. Nambiar, P.H. Parekh, R.B. Misra, S., B. H. Parekh and S.N. Shroff for the Petitioners. A.V. Rangam, for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. These two writ petitions under article 32 have been filed by the petitioners challenging the constitutional validity of section 17(1)(a), (b) and (c) of [section 16] of the [Bombay City Improvement (Amendment ) Act, 1956], as amended in 1955. The petitioners are aggrieved by the judgment of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court dismissing their writ petitions. They have filed these two writ petition under article 226 of the Constitutions.

The appellant, a worker employed in the appellant's factory, was an adult worker. He worked for about 8 hours in a week. The total number of hours of work in a month was 9 hours. On the night of 1st April, 1966, he was found to be in charge of a number of persons and was required to work under him. The appellant was also found to have been in charge thereof at the Alexandra Docks. He was served with a notice dated December 6, 1966 by the Inspector of Factories asking him to show cause why his attendance should not be terminated. On January 7, 1967, he filed an application before the Labour Officer for permission to terminate his attendance and to continue as such. The said application was rejected by the appellant on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of Rule 25(1) of the Rules. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Labour Commissioner. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions contained in Rule 25 (1) were not applicable to the case and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to continue in service as he had failed in his attendance. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The provisions contained under Rule 25 are not applicable in the case of a worker who is required to be given notice or to continue to work for more than 9 hours in any day. The provisions of sub-rule (1), therefore, were not attracted to the facts of the present case. [775 H] (ii) The appellant had been working as an adult workers at the time when he was examined by the respondent. He had worked for 8 hours and had worked under him for 8 days in a day. Therefore, he could not be said to have failed to observe the provisions relating to the hours of duty. [750 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1379 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and order dated September 25, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Special Appeal No.. 11 of 1967. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. R. N. Sachthey, for respondent No. 1. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Hegde, J. This appeal is directed against the judgment of the High court of Allahabad dated September 10, 1966 dismissing the writ application filed by the appellants. The facts leading to this appeal are these: The appellant is a worker in the factory at the hours he worked for eight hours and his work was not less than 8 hours. He has failed to give the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day. In the circumstances, the High Courts were right in holding that there was no breach of Rule 10 of the U.P. Factories Rules, 1948. [751 H] The appellant's case is covered by the decision of this Court in [The State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Ram Chandra Yadav and Ors.] , referred to. JUDGMENT: Civil Appeals Nos. 1378-1379 of 1967, 1424-1425 of 1966, 1522-1523 of 1966 and 1620-1621 of 1966 are directed against judgment dated September 20, 1966 passed by the Allahabad, High Court at Lucknow in Special Appeals No. 11 of 1966 respectively. The appellants were employed as an ordinary workmen at the said hours. They were paid wages for the period from 1st January, 1966 to 31st March, 1967. On December 6/10, 1967 they were paid a sum of Rs. 2,000/- per month. On February 9, 1968 they were given a notice under Rule 10(1)(c) of U. P. Factories (Amendment) Rules, 1967 and the said rule was amended by the U P Factories (Second Amendment) Rules 1967. The respondents filed an appeal against this amendment to the High.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in which he was residing. He filed an application for eviction under Section 20(1) of the Act on the ground that the landlord had let out the premises to him for a period of 10 years and that the tenant had not paid rent from 1.10.1970 till the date of filing of the suit. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 39 of the said Act and accordingly he dismissed the application filed by the appellant. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the Rent Controller and allowed the writ petition filed by him. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of Section 20 (1) are applicable to the premises in question during the pendency of the proceedings before the Rent Authority and therefore the benefit of the protection under the Act will not be available to the appellant because he was entitled for the benefit under Section 10(2)(i) of Act. It is further contended that the High court has erred in holding that the protection given by Section 20 is applicable only to a suit pending on the date when the suit is filed and therefore it is clear that the bar under Section 12 is not attracted. The learned counsel for the respondent-landlord supported the judgment of the High. Court. It was contended that in view of the language of Section 39, the appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions contained in Section 20 clause (1). It was further submitted that the question whether the appellant had let over the premises or not during the period of ten years is a mixed question of law and fact and therefore there is no bar for the Court to interfere with the order passed by the Rent Control Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained under Section 2(1)(e) are attracted only to an existing building where the tenant has let out or has not paid or tendered rent from a previous date but has paid or deposited rent from that date and therefore no bar is available to him to claim the benefit thereunder. [775 H] 2. The protection given under Section 19 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 is applicable to a case where the suit was instituted within 10 years of the commencement of the tenancy. [750 A] 3.1 The provisions of sub section (2) of Section 2 are attracted to an application filed under Section 11 of the Code and therefore in view thereof the bar contained in the Act would not be applicable. [751 B] 3:2. In the instant case, the question as to whether the suit has been instituted within ten years from the date on which the suit for eviction was filed or not is a pure question of fact and it cannot be said that the Court below erred in law in holding otherwise.

The appellant, a thika tenant, filed a suit for eviction of the thika tenants from the thikka premises on the ground that he was a thikkakka tenant within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) read with section 3 of the Act. The trial court held that the thica tenant had not been evicted by the execution of the decree or order passed in the suit and, therefore, the provisions of the said Act were applicable to all suits, appeals and proceedings (a) before the Controller, and (b) before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952. The appellant filed a second appeal against the order of the trial court which was dismissed by the High Court. The High Court held that in view of the provisions contained in section 4 of the West Bengal Thika tenancy (Amendment Act, 1952, the Controller had no jurisdiction to decide the matter and that the provisions regarding notice under section 4 were not applicable to the case. In this appeal it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in holding that the Controller was competent to hear the matter. The question whether a thica tenancy was liable to be terminated by the executing court or not, was decided by the trial Court and the High Courts were wrong in saying that the Act was prospective only. It is further contended that the words "any of the grounds" occurring in section 3(3) of the Bengal Thiaka Tenancy (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1952 ceased to operate on the date of institution of the suit or proceeding which might be before any court or before a competent person. The contention of the respondent was that the word "any" occurring therein was not applicable in view,of section 4 and therefore the provisions relating to notice under [section 4] were not attracted to the facts of the case and, as such, the provision regarding notice could not be applied to the suit. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that in the instant case the thija tenant had been evicted from the premises on 21st October 1952 and, consequently, the Act would apply to him. In our opinion, the High courts were wrong. Section 4 of Bengal Thiika Tenancy (Third Amendment) Act, 1953 was prospective in operation. The words " any of the ground" occurring under section 3 in order to succeed in a case where no notice under that section was necessary. The Controller had jurisdiction to determine the matter in accordance with the provisions made in the Act and he was bound to deal with all pre Act suits on the basis that no notice was necessary, and if any of them could be heard by any court, or before any person deciding such matter, the words used in section 5 were not relevant. The respondent contended that as the Controller did not have jurisdiction to hear and decide the case, the bar under section 5 was not attracted. Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was applicable to a case which might have been before the Rent Controller or the HighCourt. The provisions relating thereto are not retrospective in operation and the provisions for notice under sections 4 and 5 were applicable only to cases where no notices under section4 were necessary. In the instant appeal it was contended that since the Act did not apply to the appellant, the respondent had no right to evict the appellant from the suit premises. The point raised by the respondent in this Court was that as a result of the amendment made in section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the said provision was applicable and the Controller could not decide the question whether the provisions were applicable or not. HELD: (1) Section 4 is prospective in nature and applies to cases which might otherwise have been decided by any Court or before the commencement of the Rent Act. [675 H] The words used are "any other matter" occurring thereunder.

The respondent was appointed as a Bench Secretary in the pay scale of Rs.400 750 and he was promoted to the post of Bench Secretaries on October 1, 1975. He was promoted as Bench Secretaries Grade I with effect from October 1. 1976. On November 2, 1976, he was transferred to the High Court of Allahabad. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the order of his transfer. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order dated November 2. 1976 and directed that all Bench Secretaries in the High Courts shall be given the pay scales admissible to Section Officers. On appeal by special leave, this Court held that the classification made under the Rules was not violative of the right to have equal pay for equal work. The State Government was directed to make a proper classification between Bench Secretaries and Bench Secretaries. In the present case, all Bench Secretary Grade I was appointed in the scale of pay of Rs 400 750 and his appointment was on October 2, 1975 with effect form January 1, 1986. On December 3, 1976 the respondent filed an application before the Chief Justice for revision of his pay scale. The said application was allowed by the Chief Judge on November 2., 1976. The appellant filed a review petition before this Court which was dismissed on April 5, 1977. Thereafter, the respondent moved the High Curt in Writ Petition No. 1223 of 1977 praying that the order passed by the State Government be quashed and the writ petitioner should be granted pay scale admissible to the Section Officers with effect on and from January 1. 1986. The learned Single Judge allowed the application holding that the respondent was entitled to get the pay Scale admissible to him as per the Rules. On further appeal, the Division Bench of the High (Court) held that there was no infirmity in the order. In this Court, it was contended by the appellant that the State had not made any classification between the Bench Secretaries or Bench Secretaries with effect prior to January 1., 1986 and that the said classification was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that there is no infirmity either in law or in fact in the decision of the State. [775 H] (2) The respondent was not entitled to claim pay scale as per Rules. He could have been granted pay scales as per rules. [750 A] (3) The classification made by the High Power Committee under the rules is not violative either of Article 16 or Article 14. [751 B] (4) The State has not made a proper discrimination between Bench Secretary and Bench Secretary. [75 H; 75 C] (5) The principle of equal pay as enshrined in Article 14 applies to all persons who are appointed to the posts of Bench Secretary, but they cannot be treated as members of the same class or category of persons. [76 D] (6) The appellant was not justified in contending that there were no rules for grant of higher pay scale and that it is only a case of discrimination. The Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the development and administration of Special Areas through Special Area Development Authorities. Section 2 of the Act provided that "the provisions of this Act shall be in conflict with the powers conferred on the Central Government by or under the Act". The Act was amended by the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Amendment) Act, 1976, which came into force on 1st April, 1976 and the words "and the owner of any land" were substituted for the words 'owner of any other land'. Section 2(1)(a) of the Amendment Act, which was introduced by the amending Act of 1976, provided that: "(a) The provisions of sections 129 and 133 of the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act shall apply to the Special Area development Authority; (b) the provisions of section 127A of the said Act shall not apply to any area other than a declared industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act." Section 127A was introduced in the Madhya Pradeshiya Act by the Amendment. The Statement of Objects and Reasons for the Amending Act, inter alia, stated that: "The main object behind the enactment of section 2 of Act No. 1 of 1976 is to provide a measure of erosion of the legislative competence of the State legislature under Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II, and that the said law was in conflict With the powers of the Central Legislature under the said entry. The power conferred on Parliament by Entry 24 of List II is not in any way affected by the declaration made by the Parliament in respect of a declared Industry under the Industrial Development and Regulation Act." The Statement further stated that the object behind enactment of the amending act was to provide an additional area for the purpose of erosion, which would ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The statement further stated: "In order to ensure rationalisation of the control of the Union Government under the [Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act], it is necessary that the provisions in the said Acts should be made by Parliament and that it should be implemented by the Central or State Legislature. It was also stated that if any law is passed by the appropriate legislature, it should have the same force as an enactment of a competent legislature." The statement of Objects & Reasons for amending the Act, particularly, the Statement of objects and reasons for the Amendment, clearly indicated that the power to impose property tax was not in conflict. The Court held that the legislation was in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act of 1957 and the State law was void. The High Court accordingly dismissed the writ petition filed by the respondent. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned Act was passed by Parliament after the amendment of section 69 of the Indian Electricity (Development & Regulation) Amendment Act. It is submitted that the amending power of the Parliament under Entry 24 was not available to the State Government and, therefore, the impugned legislation was invalid. The learned counsel for the respondent contended that the amendments made in the [Madhya Pradesh Municipalities (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act] 1976 were valid and the provisions relating to development and the administration of the Municipal Corporations were also valid. It may be mentioned that the amendment made by section 69(d) of Act, 1975 was not applicable to the case before us. The question whether the impugned enactment is in conflict or not has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [501F] In the instant case, the amendments were made by Act No, 1 of 1977 and the amending law was passed in exercise of the powers under Entry 42 of List III read with entry 24, list II, of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The amendment made in section 69 (d) was not challenged before this Court.

The Mineral Concession Rules of 1949 were framed by the Government under section 3 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948. The appellants' case was that they had leased out their lands to the State Government for a period exceeding one year. They submitted an application for renewal of the lease on or before July 1, 1945, and the same was rejected by the Deputy Commissioner, who held that the lease was not valid. On appeal, the Board of Revenue confirmed the order of the Deputy Collector. The matter was carried to the High Court in a writ petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of section 20(1) of the Mineral Concessions Rules were attracted and the lease could not be terminated by giving three months' notice. On further appeal, this Court held that there was no valid ground for terminating the lease and that the Deputy Secretary to Government in the Department of Mines and Geology had no power to terminate the lease. The question whether the lease should be terminated or not was left open. In the present case, the appellants were directed to pay compensation as per the third proviso to section 20 (1) and on that basis compensation would be payable under section 20 of the Act. The Court held: "The second proviso to sub section (1), however, does not apply in the case of any right created after July 1 1945, but it applies only to cases where the rights were created before July I, 1945 for a total period exceeding two years and falling under the second proviso." In the result, the appeal was allowed. The State Government filed an application under Article 227 of the constitution. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The High court was wrong in holding that there is no valid reason for terminating lease by giving two months' previous notice. [775 H] (b) The words "such rights" in section 20 are not applicable to cases of any land created by a landholder on or after the 1st day of July, 1945. Section 20(2) does not refer to the rights created after that date but only refers to those rights which were created after the date of the notification. [750 H] The words 'such rights' in section 10(1)(b) are not relevant for determining whether the right was created before or after July I 1945. [751 A] (c) The word "such" in the second Proviso to section 10 (1). does not mean that the terms of the proviso should be construed as referring to those things which were intended to be mentioned in the first proviso. [75 H; 75 B] (d) The expression "such right" in sub section 2(b) means that the right created before the 1-7- 1945, is a vested right and not a vested interest. [76 D] (e) The second Proviso does not cover cases where there is any land which was created after August 7, 1945 but it refers to cases which were not intended to have been mentioned in sub sections 2(a), 2(c). [778 G] (f) The proviso to s. 10(2)(b), therefore, cannot be read as referring only to those matters which were meant to be included in the third Proviso and not to the second provisos.
